items.title: Testing TLS 1.3 PQC on constrained devices and microcontrollers
items.summary: The UK, EU and US governments have set timelines for post-quantum cryptography migration of critical systems, with deadlines ranging from 2028 to 2035. This paper focuses on IoT-class devices and microcontrollers and the viability of using PQC to connect these devices in secure TLS 1.3 connections. Using wolfSSL, we benchmark a 36-combination TLS 1.3 algorithm matrix, pairing ML-KEM-512/768/1024 and X25519/ECC P-256 key exchange with ML-DSA-44/65/87, Ed25519, ECDSA, and RSA-PSS authentication, across four devices (Raspberry Pi Pico W & Pico 2 W, ESP32, and a Raspberry Pi Zero), measuring both handshake latency and energy consumption. We found that in capable devices, all choices in the TLS matrix gave similar results, but that in IoT-class devices, PQC performance is highly implementation- and architecture-dependent: the common assumption that elliptic-curve key exchange must be cheaper than post-quantum lattice-based key exchange does not hold in this wolfSSL-based implementation, where the best full-PQC combination (ML-KEM-512 + ML-DSA-44) completes TLS handshakes 41% faster than the equivalent classical-modern pairing (X25519 + RSA-PSS) on the Pico W (up to 2.12x as energy-efficient, depending on the paired authentication algorithm), and 8.9x faster on the ESP32. Full-PQC, ML-KEM-512/ML-DSA-44, is not only possible but energy-competitive with or superior to Hybrid or Elliptic Curve alternatives on the most constrained devices, though ML-DSA's variable signing time means applications with strict latency-predictability budgets must accept this variance as the cost of full quantum-safe authentication. We further show that the IETF's draft-specified X25519+ML-KEM-768 hybrid incurs approximately the combined cost of its two components, rather than offering a performance compromise, making pure ML-KEM the more practical choice on hardware lacking Curve25519 assembly support.

items.title: Make the Adversary Spend More Energy: Generative Deception against Language-Model Attackers in Critical Infrastructure
items.summary: Language-model attackers consume computational resources as they explore and interact with a target, creating an opportunity for cyber deception to impose costs. Whether such engagements favor the defender requires measuring both sides. We evaluate an autonomous language-model attacker against a decoy that uses a defending language model to analyze attacker commands and select defensive responses. Across 330 sessions, eight model pairs, two attacker profiles and three counter-injection levels, both sides run on identical GPUs and their energy is measured above idle. With runtime thinking disabled, the attacker-to-defender energy ratio has a 95% interval above one in 41 of 48 configurations under an allocation excluding attacker diagnostic calls, and in all 48 when those calls are included. Token ratios remain within approximately a factor of two in configurations without generation-cap truncation, showing that token counts can obscure substantial energy asymmetry. Counter-injection increases attacker tokens by approximately 9% per level without a detectable pooled change in energy consumption. Enabling thinking on both sides increases defender energy by 8--17 times and reverses the exchange for one model pair in the original campaign. We use these findings to motivate a proposed SCADA deception architecture with private physical state per identified adversary and deterministic protocol and process emulation.

items.title: Privacy Accounting for Empirical Denoisers
items.summary: Diffusion models have emerged as the foundation of modern generative systems, yet their high memorization capacity raises privacy concerns. While differentially private (DP) training provides formal guarantees, it comes at a cost in sample quality. In this work, we study a complementary question: how much privacy loss is incurred during the sampling process itself? Directly analyzing modern neural denoisers is challenging because their sensitivity to a single training example is generally intractable. To overcome this challenge, we construct and analyze a clipped privacy-accountable empirical denoiser, a training-free estimator of the Bayes-optimal denoiser, whose per-step sensitivity can be computed explicitly, allowing each denoising step to be a Gaussian mechanism. This perspective enables privacy accounting under Gaussian DP when each training example contributes to each denoising step, and under $f$-DP trade-off functions when each generated sample uses a single randomly subsampled block of the training data. We report every $(\varepsilon, δ)$ guarantee as a certified upper bound from a privacy loss distribution accountant, and use a cumulant-based Edgeworth approximation as a fast diagnostic, characterizing where it is reliable and where it becomes anti-conservative. We also analyze the privacy loss along the denoising trajectory and show that it grows steeply near the critical window in which semantic content is formed. This observation motivates hybrid samplers that use the private empirical denoiser through the formative steps where it remains a faithful proxy for the neural denoiser, then switch to a public neural denoiser for the remaining refinement. Our results on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64 show that the privacy of diffusion models depends not only on the training procedure, but also on sampling-time design choices such as subsampling, stopping time, and hybrid denoising.

items.title: The app/process-api-response-headers action accepts fake Craft API response headers from any...
items.summary:
The app/process-api-response-headers action accepts fake Craft API response headers from any authenticated control panel user.



A non-admin user with only accessCp can place newline characters in X-Craft-Plugin-Licenses. Craft passes this value to its .env writer without removing the newlines.

items.title: Craft CMS allows any authenticated control panel user to submit an element-search condition whose...
items.summary:
Craft CMS allows any authenticated control panel user to submit an element-search condition whose element selector is evaluated as a sandboxed Twig object template. Craft’s allowed column filter delegates property lookup to Yii ArrayHelper, outside Twig’s SecurityPolicy. Repeated single-segment lookups therefore bypass the sandbox’s empty property/method allowlists.



The vulnerable condition value is ultimately cast to an integer. That does not protect the secret: the template can return author ID 1 when a guessed key character is correct and an impossible ID otherwise. The JSON endpoint returns entries for the first case and an empty array for the second, forming a stable remote character oracle.



After recovering GeneralConfig::securityKey, the same user can compute Craft’s generic HMAC wire format offline. Signed parameters such as redirect are then accepted and passed to unsandboxed View::renderObjectTemplate(), where Twig’s string-callable form can invoke native PHP callables. The regression proof uses the harmless substr() callback and observes abcdef becoming cdef; it does not execute an OS command.

items.title: filelock: ReadWriteLock on the hard-link route deletes any directory another user renames onto its .filelock-* link directory name
items.summary:
`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) remove their private `.filelock-*` link directories with `shutil.rmtree` (a recursive delete) on a remembered path. They do not check that the path still names the directory they created. This happens on the hard-link route (a hard link is a second name for the same file). That route is every connection on macOS since 4.1.1 and any POSIX process without a usable `/proc/self/fd` (a Linux path that names the process's own open files), such as a chroot or container that does not mount `/proc`.

Another local user who can rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can rename one of the directories of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the link directory's name, or onto a forged dead-holder name. Such a lock directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The lock user's process then deletes that tree and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and reports no error. Stock Linux with `/proc` mounted is not affected. Affected versions are filelock 4.1.0 through 4.2.0.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-LSSZIUEO` [high, CWE-367]: ReadWriteLock deletes any directory another user renames to .filelock-*.

Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user rename in a non-sticky shared parent that turns private-link cleanup into recursive deletion of the lock user's tree. The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism, notes that the macOS route rests on a Linux run with `/proc` hidden rather than on a run on macOS, and narrows the finding to that precondition and route.

items.title: filelock: ReadWriteLock on Windows acts on SQLite side files another local user places beside its database
items.summary:
On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: `<database>-journal`, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); `<database>-wal`, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and `<database>-shm`, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone `DELETE` on it, which a file's creator may do. `C:\Windows\Temp` (the temporary directory of services, granting `BUILTIN\Users` create but not delete) and `C:\Users\Public` are such directories.

With a `-wal` in place, every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at once, whatever `timeout` says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a `-journal` beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). It is not among the findings of the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 3.3 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): create one file beside the database and set its ACL (access control list); no race, and the other account can place the file days earlier. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account that can create files in the directory is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other account learns nothing. `I:N` (no integrity impact in the scored variant): see the scoring note. `A:L` (partial availability impact): every acquire fails with an exception that `Timeout` handlers do not catch, until the other account removes its file; no crash, and the lock's own data is not changed.

Scoring note. The deletion variant reads `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L` (3.6): `I:L` because the lock user's process deletes one file the journal names, `AC:H` because it needs a lock database that holds a table, which filelock does not create, and a journal the lock user can open for writing. The lower-reading rule of this advisory set scores the variant that reaches every `ReadWriteLock` on Windows in such a directory, 3.3, and describes the deletion variant under Mechanism. Classification from the review: **security** (another account), availability for the scored variant.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`, both of which connect through `_connect`. On Linux and macOS the lock takes other routes, covered by GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.
- Directory: one where another account can create files but cannot delete the lock user's. `C:\Windows\Temp` carries `BUILTIN\Users:(CI)(S,WD,AD,X)` (create file and create subdirectory, no delete child); `C:\Users\Public` and any directory with such an entry qualify. A directory only the lock user can write, such as `%LOCALAPPDATA%` or the per-user temporary directory, is not affected.
- The other account creates `<database>-wal`, grants everyone modify and denies everyone `DELETE` on it. A file's creator may set both. The lock user can open and read the file but not delete it.

items.title: virtualenv: Temporary app-data can leave dangling seed package links
items.summary:
## Summary

The app-data seeder can leave an environment linked to temporary package files that virtualenv deletes when creation
finishes. The environment-variable and configuration-file forms of `symlink_app_data` can enable this state even though
the command-line flag is disabled for temporary app-data. The resulting environment depends on a cache pathname that its
owner no longer controls.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-ZOE2GEPC` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.
This draft records source review and functional remediation checks. The reporter's cross-account code-execution claim
has not been independently reproduced.

## Affected area

Integrity of app-data references after temporary cache cleanup.

## Attacker-controlled input

Symlink seeding must be enabled through `VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA` or `symlink_app_data` in the configuration file,
and app-data setup must fall back to a temporary directory. A missing or unwritable configured cache can cause that
fallback. Ordinary copy seeding does not leave these references.

The security concern requires a shared temporary-directory parent where another account can acquire the deleted cache
pathname, followed by use of the affected environment. That account need not already be able to modify the environment
or the private cache while it exists. This differs from the security policy's excluded case of an account that already
controls live app-data contents. On a platform with a temporary-directory parent private to the environment owner, that
cross-account condition is absent. Windows functional checks do not establish cross-account exposure under Windows
defaults.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[symlink seeder](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/embed/via_app_data/via_app_data.py),
[temporary cache cleanup](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/app_data/via_tempdir.py).

## Mechanism

When app-data setup falls back to a temporary directory, the command-line `--symlink-app-data` action is disabled. A
value supplied by `VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA` or `virtualenv.ini` can still become the parser default, and the seeder
constructor accepts that value without rechecking the cache lifetime. It links `site-packages/pip` into the temporary
cache. Session cleanup deletes that cache, leaving a dangling link whose pathname can later be claimed by another
account on a shared temporary filesystem.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner ran its reproduction as two unprivileged users, with root used only to switch identities. The environment
owner had an unwritable home, so app-data fell back to `/tmp`. The control used the command-line flag and received a
real pip directory. With `VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA=1`, the new environment instead contained a `pip` link into a
deleted `/tmp/tmpXXXXXXXX` directory. A second uid recreated the target path and placed a fake `pip/__init__.py` there.
When the owner ran `venv/bin/pip --version`, that module created a marker inside the owner's environment and printed
`this is not pip`.

The cross-account path requires a shared temporary parent, a second account able to claim the deleted name, and later
use of the environment. A private temporary parent removes that route. The report traces the incomplete temporary-cache
guard to #1661, first released in 20.0.6.
[Public fix PR #3437](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3437) copies packages whenever app-data is
temporary, whatever supplied the symlink option. The implementation review checked the remediation; it did not rerun the
cross-account reproduction.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Environment owner
    participant V as virtualenv seeder
    participant T as Temporary app-data in /tmp
    participant E as site-packages/pip link
    participant A as Other local acco

finishes. The environment-variable and configuration-file forms of `symlink_app_data` can enable this state even though
the command-line flag is disabled for temporary app-data. The resulting environment depends on a cache pathname that its
owner no longer controls.

items.title: virtualenv: Pip seeding with download omits wheel digest verification
items.summary:
## Summary

The pip seeder acquires bundled wheels with download=False and lets pip access the index when --download is selected.
Index candidates on that path do not pass through virtualenv's wheel digest verification.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-74ALJBUF` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Wheel selection by the pip seeder when downloads are enabled.

## Attacker-controlled input

The pip seeder and download option must be selected. The finding concerns the default-index digest-verification policy.
Explicit custom-index settings already opt out of comparison against PyPI metadata; this patch retains that policy.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[pip seeder](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/embed/pip_invoke.py).

## Mechanism

With `--seeder pip --download`, `PipInvoke.get_pip_install_cmd()` first calls `get_wheel(download=False)`, so
virtualenv's `download_wheel()` and `verify_wheel_digest()` are skipped. It then lets `pip install` consult the
configured index. An index wheel with the same package and version as the bundled wheel can be selected without
virtualenv comparing its SHA-256 with PyPI metadata. The default app-data seeder takes the verification path for the
same option.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner built a local index named in `pip.conf` that served a modified copy of the bundled pip wheel under the same
filename. In the control run, `virtualenv --download env-default` rejected the wheel with a digest mismatch. In the
second run, adding `--seeder pip` produced an environment whose installed `pip/__init__.py` matched the index wheel;
`env-pip/bin/pip --version` ran the added line. The reproducer checked the installed bytes and marker before reporting
`BUG`.

Both `--seeder pip` and `--download` are needed. The report used a non-PyPI index from `pip.conf` and left
`PIP_INDEX_URL`, `PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL`, and `PIP_INDEX` unset, so virtualenv's default-seeder PyPI comparison remained
active. This does not establish index control in the default PyPI setup. The unchecked pip-seeder download path is
older, while the comparison with the default seeder arose when digest verification was added in 21.7.12.
[PR #3430](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3430) acquires and verifies selected wheels before invoking pip with
index lookup disabled.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant I as Index in pip.conf
    participant V as virtualenv PipInvoke
    participant P as pip install
    participant E as Seeded environment
    I->>V: serve modified pip wheel
    V->>V: get_wheel(download=False)
    V->>P: install with --download permitting index lookup
    P->>I: select same-version index wheel
    I->>E: modified pip installed without virtualenv digest check
    E->>E: later pip invocation runs added code
    Note over V,E: Default app-data seeder rejects the same digest
```

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-74ALJBUF`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

items.title: virtualenv: Downloaded wheel selection and caching precede verification
items.summary:
## Summary

Wheel downloads go directly into the reusable wheelhouse, while the verification target is selected from pip's textual
output. A verification failure does not remove the downloaded file from that cache.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-ST00DRO3` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Download selection and promotion into the reusable wheel cache.

## Attacker-controlled input

A download must fail verification, or the archive selected from pip output must differ from the file later reused.
Default-index digest verification must be enabled. Existing custom-index exceptions are outside the promised PyPI
comparison.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[wheel download and digest check](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/wheels/acquire.py).

`download_wheel()` tells pip to write directly into the reusable `wheel/house` cache. It then selects a path to hash
from the first `Saved ` line in pip's stdout, rather than from the file pip actually placed there. A package index can
inject such a line through a discarded link's `data-requires-python` attribute. A separate failure exists without the
forged line: a digest mismatch raises after the downloaded wheel has entered the cache, and the rejected bytes remain
there. Later wheel selection does not hash the cached file again.

reproduction used a known absolute path to the genuine bundled wheel; that prerequisite is part of this variant.

[PR #3430](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3430) downloads to a private temporary directory, verifies the actual
archive, and promotes it only after acceptance.

    participant P as pip download
    participant C as wheel/house cache
    participant V as virtualenv digest check
    participant N as New environment

    P-->>V: stdout names genuine bundled wheel
    V->>V: hash genuine wheel and accept

items.title: virtualenv: Xonsh activation literals depend on the script decoding codec
items.summary:
## Summary

Caller-supplied prompt text can become executable syntax in the xonsh activation script. An attacker must influence the
value passed to virtualenv, and a user must subsequently activate the environment.

## Affected area

Xonsh reads a UTF-8 activation script using a legacy multibyte encoding such as GBK. Printable non-ASCII bytes can
change how the reader recognizes an adjacent quote. The report concerns POSIX activation. It does not establish exposure
through unrelated activators.

## Attacker-controlled input

The attacker controls prompt or destination data passed as a virtualenv argument. The user later sources the generated
activation script.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[xonsh quote()](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/xonsh/__init__.py),
[UTF-8 template writer](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/via_template.py).

## Mechanism

The generator writes `activate.xsh` as UTF-8. Its `quote()` used `repr()`, which leaves printable non-ASCII characters
in the file and backslash-escapes an embedded quote. Xonsh's `source` reads the file using `$XONSH_ENCODING`. With GBK
or Big5, the UTF-8 bytes of `中` end in `0xad`, which pairs with the following `0x5c` backslash as one decoded character.
The backslash no longer escapes the quote. A prompt containing both quote kinds can then close its Python string literal
and supply statements that run during activation. With UTF-8 source decoding, the same value stays inside the literal.

## Reproduction and evidence

The original scanner finding, `ANT-2026-PAUVP7YL`, demonstrated this byte-level failure in `activate_this.py`: a hostile
prompt loaded through `exec(open(file).read(), ...)` under GBK created a marker, while UTF-8 and `runpy.run_path`
controls did not. The xonsh path in this advisory was identified in the subsequent maintainer-provided review.
[PR #3432](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3432) shows the xonsh source-decoding chain and changes `quote()` to
`ascii()`, which writes non-ASCII characters as escapes. Its regression test encodes the generated literal as ASCII,
decodes it as GBK, and checks that `ast.literal_eval` returns the original prompt.

The attack needs control of the prompt or destination value, an affected xonsh source encoding, and later sourcing of
the generated file. The original `activate_this.py` reproducer does not itself prove xonsh execution; that result is
attributed to the separate review. Existing `activate.xsh` files must be regenerated after the fix.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prompt supplier
    participant V as virtualenv quote()
    participant F as activate.xsh bytes
    participant X as xonsh source
    A->>V: 中 plus escaped quote and statements
    V->>F: repr writes UTF-8 中 followed by backslash
    alt XONSH_ENCODING is UTF-8
        F->>X: backslash remains an escape
        X-->>A: prompt remains data
    else XONSH_ENCODING is GBK or Big5
        F->>X: decoder consumes backslash as trail byte
        X->>X: quote closes and statements run
    end
    Note over V,X: ascii() emits only ASCII bytes and preserves the literal
```

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-PAUVP7YL`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from shutil import rmtree

work = Path("/tmp/activate-this-gbk")
rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True)

env_dir = work / "venv"

items.title: virtualenv: Seeded files retain permissions from an older cache
items.summary:
## Summary

The app-data copy seeder uses shutil.copy, which preserves cached file modes independently of the current umask. A cache
populated under permissive permissions can therefore produce files with wider access in later environments.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-487MH6OW` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Permissions of files copied from app-data into a new environment.

## Attacker-controlled input

The cache must contain files created with broader permissions than the current environment creator intends. Another
account must also be able to traverse the new environment and reach those files. A private parent directory prevents
that access. No control of a private live cache is assumed.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[copy helpers](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/util/path/_sync.py).

## Mechanism

The default app-data seeder extracts a wheel into a reusable cache and copies its files into later environments with
`shutil.copy()`. That function applies the cached source mode to each destination file after creating it, overriding the
current run's umask. If the cache image was built under umask `000`, a later environment created under umask `022` can
receive mode-`0666` pip files. The cache may be private while the new environment is reachable by other local accounts.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner created two histories with separate private app-data caches. In the control, the owner's first run used
umask `022`; a later environment had no files writable by another account, and that account could not append to
`pip/__init__.py`. In the attack history, the first run used umask `000` and the later run still used `022`. The report
counted 478 of 493 environment files writable by others. A second unprivileged uid appended a line to pip, and
`bin/pip --version` ran it as the environment owner. The cache itself remained under a mode-`0700` home in both
histories.

An attacker cannot force the owner's earlier umask through this finding; the attack also needs a traversable
destination. A mode-`002` cache can expose group write access under suitable group permissions. The scanner dates
app-data copy seeding to #1578, first released in 20.0.2. [PR #3425](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3425)
creates copied files under a fixed non-writable-by-others policy further restricted by the current umask.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Environment owner
    participant C as Private app-data cache
    participant E as Later environment
    participant A as Other local account
    U->>C: first seed extraction under umask 000
    C-->>U: cached pip files have mode 0666
    U->>E: create environment under umask 022
    C->>E: shutil.copy reapplies mode 0666
    A->>E: append code to pip/__init__.py
    U->>E: run bin/pip --version
    E-->>U: appended code runs as owner
```

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-487MH6OW`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

from pathlib import Path

sys.stdout.reconfigure(line_buffering=True)  # keep these lines in order with those of the child processes

items.title: virtualenv: Bash prompt values can change meaning under older compatibility modes
items.summary:
## Summary

Caller-supplied prompt text can become executable syntax in the bash activation prompt. An attacker must influence the
value passed to virtualenv, and a user must subsequently activate the environment and draw the prompt.

## Affected area

Bash runs with compatibility level 4.2 and draws the environment prompt. Its replacement-string behavior differs from
newer compatibility modes, leaving prompt text subject to a second interpretation. The report concerns POSIX activation.
It does not establish exposure through unrelated activators.

## Attacker-controlled input

The attacker controls prompt or destination data passed as a virtualenv argument. The user later sources the generated
activation script.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[bash prompt assembly](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh).

## Mechanism

`bin/activate` copies the prompt into `PS1`. A shell expands `PS1` again when it draws a prompt, so the value must
survive both the assignment and that later expansion. The bash and zsh branches escape for their usual prompt rules.
Three other paths still interpret prompt data as commands: dash sourcing `activate` directly, a child dash inheriting an
exported `PS1` from bash, and bash running at compatibility level 4.2 or lower. A value such as `x$(touch MARKER)y` then
runs `touch` on prompt display. Creating the environment does not run the payload.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner's child-shell reproducer creates an environment with `--prompt 'x$(touch MARKER)y'`, sources `bin/activate`
in interactive bash, and starts interactive `sh` (dash). Its control leaves `PS1` unexported: neither shell creates
`MARKER`. With `PS1` exported, bash displays the prompt without executing the value, but the child dash creates
`MARKER`; the reproducer ends in `BUG`. The report gives separate console reproductions for direct dash activation and
bash compatibility level 4.2. The child-shell path can arise after another environment's activation has exported `PS1`.

The scanner linked this finding to [#3326](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3326) and its follow-up #3390. Those
changes cover the usual bash path but leave the three paths above. The proposed change in
[#3418](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3418) keeps a variable reference in `PS1`, so prompt text is expanded as
data when drawn. The private report's reproducer was run by the scanner; the later command-execution result was supplied
by the maintainer review. This advisory does not claim that every POSIX shell or every bash mode is affected.

## Introduced

The report traces direct dash sourcing to the first 20.x activator (20.0.0b1), and inherited `PS1` to #3390 (first
released in 21.14.7). It demonstrates the compatibility-level case on bash 5.2. Those historical boundaries come from
the report; the release confirmed by the maintainer is 21.14.8.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prompt supplier
    participant V as virtualenv
    participant B as Interactive bash
    participant D as Child dash
    A->>V: --prompt x$(touch MARKER)y
    V->>B: generated bin/activate
    B->>B: assign escaped prompt to PS1
    alt PS1 is not exported
        B->>D: start sh with its own PS1
        D-->>B: marker absent
    else PS1 is exported
        B->>D: start sh with inherited PS1
        D->>D: expand $(touch MARKER) on prompt draw
        D-->>B: marker created
    end
```

are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

items.title: virtualenv: Venv configuration readback can reinterpret path boundaries
items.summary:
## Summary

The venv creator reads the standard library's generated pyvenv.cfg with splitlines() and merges all resulting keys over
virtualenv's configuration. Line-boundary characters from destination data can therefore become configuration structure
before output sanitization.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-6ZQHJ6VI` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Configuration readback by the stdlib venv creator.

## Attacker-controlled input

An untrusted caller must influence the destination pathname passed to the venv creator. That pathname must contain a
character that Python treats as a line boundary. The builtin creator follows a different configuration-writing path.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[venv readback](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/via_global_ref/venv.py),
[configuration parser](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/pyenv_cfg.py).

## Mechanism

With `--creator venv`, virtualenv asks the standard library to create an environment, reads its `pyvenv.cfg` with
`str.splitlines()`, and merges the parsed keys over virtualenv's chosen settings. CPython writes the destination into a
`command =` value without escaping every character that `splitlines()` recognizes as a line boundary. A destination
containing U+2028, for example, can therefore supply new `home` and `include-system-site-packages` keys during readback.
Virtualenv writes those keys as real configuration lines. The builtin creator does not use this readback path.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner used one destination value with U+2028 between `home = /attacker/chosen`,
`include-system-site-packages = true`, and an absorbing `x =` key. A `python -m venv --without-pip` control kept the
value inside its `command` line and reported the base interpreter's `sys._home`. `virtualenv --creator venv --no-seed`
on the same value wrote separate injected configuration lines and its interpreter reported
`sys._home = /attacker/chosen`. The path did not require a literal newline byte. The control establishes that the extra
keys came from virtualenv's readback, not from the standard library's initial file alone.

The altered `home` can change which standard-library files the interpreter loads if an attacker also controls that
location; `include-system-site-packages = true` weakens environment isolation. Choosing the venv creator is required,
either explicitly or through a rare fallback. The report traces the readback to the 20.x rewrite, first released in
20.0.0b1. [PR #3426](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3426) rejects line-boundary characters before creation and
rebuilds the final configuration from selected settings.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Destination supplier
    participant S as stdlib venv
    participant V as virtualenv readback
    participant C as Final pyvenv.cfg
    participant P as Environment Python
    A->>S: path contains U+2028 and home = /attacker/chosen
    S->>C: write path inside command value
    V->>C: read with splitlines()
    V->>V: parse suffix as separate keys
    V->>C: rewrite home and include-system-site-packages
    P->>C: read injected keys on startup
    C-->>P: sys._home changes and isolation is disabled
```

items.title: virtualenv: Seed replacement does not contain metadata deletion paths
items.summary:
## Summary

The app-data seeder joins paths from existing distribution metadata to site-packages and deletes the resulting paths
without checking containment within the environment.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-SXOEHWP7` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Removal of a previously installed seed package.

## Attacker-controlled input

An environment being reused must contain distribution metadata influenced by another account. The invoking user must
have deletion rights over the paths named by that metadata. Installing a new environment without existing package
metadata does not enter this cleanup path.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[seed uninstall](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/embed/via_app_data/pip_install/base.py).

## Mechanism

Before reinstalling a seed wheel, `PipInstall._uninstall_previous_version()` accepts an existing `pip-*.dist-info`
directory in the destination. `_uninstall_dist()` reads its `top_level.txt` and `RECORD`, joins each entry to
`site-packages`, and deletes the result. It does not check whether `..`, an absolute entry, or a linked parent takes the
path outside the environment. The default app-data seeder reaches this path when it reuses a tree containing
seed-package metadata; `--clear` removes that tree first.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner prepared a project with `.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/pip-1.0.dist-info/`. Its `top_level.txt`
contained `../../../../../Documents`; its `RECORD` named `../../../../../notes.txt,,`. The user's home initially held
`Documents/thesis/chapter1.txt` and `notes.txt`. Running `virtualenv .venv` exited successfully but removed both paths.
A control tree with `top_level.txt` set to `pip` and a normal `pip/__init__.py` RECORD entry left the home files in
place. The reproducer prints `BUG` only when the control files survive and both attack targets disappear.

The deletion uses the invoking user's permissions and runs during creation, before any use of the environment. It
requires an existing destination that another account could populate; a fresh empty environment does not supply hostile
metadata. The report traces this cleanup to #2186, first released in 20.8.1.
[PR #3428](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3428) checks each deletion path against the resolved environment root
and refuses to delete the root itself.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prepared .venv metadata
    participant V as App-data seeder
    participant P as site-packages
    participant H as User home
    A->>P: top_level.txt names ../../../../../Documents
    A->>P: RECORD names ../../../../../notes.txt
    V->>P: read pip-1.0.dist-info before reinstall
    P->>H: join entries without containment check
    V->>H: remove Documents and notes.txt
    V-->>A: virtualenv exits successfully
```

items.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unhandled error on excessive content-encodings
items.summary:
### Impact

undici's `fetch()` crashes the Node.js process when a malicious server returns a response with more than five content codings and closes the connection before sending the body. undici rejects such responses (a content-encoding limit), but it created the internal response stream before that check and returned without attaching an error listener or aborting the request. The early close then surfaces a content-length mismatch on that orphaned internal stream, which Node.js treats as an unhandled `error` and terminates the process. A remote, unauthenticated server can trigger this with a single response, even when the application correctly catches the `fetch()` rejection. undici 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x are affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`. undici now validates the content-encoding chain before creating the internal body stream and aborts the response when the limit is exceeded, so no error can surface on an orphaned stream.

### Workarounds

None.

items.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unbounded memory in the EventSource parser
items.summary:
### Impact

undici's `EventSource` client can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised Server-Sent Events peer. By sending millions of tiny completed `data:` fields with no blank event separator, or a single unfinished line split across many chunks, the parser retains a growing amount of per-field and per-chunk state. The byte-based `maxEventSize` and `maxResponseSize` limits do not bound that retained state, and `maxResponseSize` is enforced on the compressed body before decompression, so a small compressed response can expand into enough retained memory to terminate the process. The application only needs to maintain an `EventSource` connection to an untrusted peer, which controls only the response. Availability is the only impact.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`, which bound the retained EventSource parser state (the number of `data` fields and buffered chunks, the unfinished-line length, and per-field byte totals) independently of the byte limits.

### Workarounds

None.

items.title: undici vulnerable to Subresource Integrity bypass via non-lowercase algorithm tokens
items.summary:
### Impact

undici's `fetch()` verifies Subresource Integrity (SRI) metadata by looking up the algorithm token in a lowercase-only set, but the SRI specification defines a valid token by its ASCII-lowercase form. A correct but non-lowercase token such as `SHA256-...` or `Sha256-...` is therefore treated as unknown and skipped. When no recognized algorithm remains, undici treats the integrity list as empty and accepts the response, so a server that returns a body different from the pinned digest passes the check.

An application that pins a response with a valid uppercase or mixed-case SRI token receives attacker-controlled bytes with no integrity error. The attacker needs only to control the response body, not the application's integrity metadata. The issue affects response integrity only. The regression was introduced in undici 7.15.0; releases 7.14.0 and earlier lowercase the token and are not affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `7.30.1` or `8.12.2`. undici now normalizes the algorithm token to ASCII lowercase before validating it and before selecting the strongest algorithm, so case variants of SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 are verified correctly.

### Workarounds

Use lowercase algorithm tokens (`sha256`, `sha384`, `sha512`) in `integrity` metadata.

items.title: multer vulnerable to Denial of Service via a pending asynchronous fileFilter after request teardown
items.summary:
### Impact

When `multer` is configured with an asynchronous `fileFilter`, a single request can crash the Node.js process. If a request is aborted (for example when one file is rejected) while another file's async `fileFilter` is still pending, the pending callback later resumes a parsing stream that multer has already torn down. busboy then emits an error on a stream that no longer has an error listener, which Node raises as an unhandled `'error'` event, and the process exits. A single unauthenticated request is enough, so any application using `multer` with an asynchronous `fileFilter` is affected, regardless of storage engine. Uploads using a synchronous `fileFilter` are not affected.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to `multer` `2.5.0` or later.

### Workarounds

Use a synchronous `fileFilter`.

items.title: Happy DOM: Incomplete fix for CVE-2026-33943: unsanitized import alias leads to host code execution
items.summary:
## Summary

The ESM compiler in `happy-dom@20.14.5` does not validate imported local binding aliases before interpolating them into generated JavaScript.

As a result, an invalid ESM import alias can be transformed into a valid JavaScript destructuring default initializer and executed.

This appears to be an alternate injection path and incomplete remediation of GHSA-6q6h-j7hj-3r64 / CVE-2026-33943. The previous fix validates `importName` in the local `export { ... }` handler, but the named import handler still places an unvalidated `alias` directly into code context.

These issues were confirmed through the public `Window` and `<script type="module">` APIs using the published `happy-dom` npm package. The PoC reaches the Node.js host `process`, obtains `node:fs`, and creates a proof directory on the host filesystem.

## Confirmed affected versions

The PoC was directly tested against:

- `happy-dom@17.0.0`
- `happy-dom@20.0.0`
- `happy-dom@20.1.0`
- `happy-dom@20.14.5`

The same PoC does not trigger on `happy-dom@16.8.1`.

The ESM compiler was introduced by commit `7bc831df2`, first released in `v17.0.0`. The vulnerable interpolation remains present through `v20.14.5`, the latest release at the time of testing.

Suggested affected range:

```text
>= 17.0.0, <= 20.14.5
```

No patched version is currently available.

## Preconditions

- JavaScript evaluation is enabled with `enableJavaScriptEvaluation: true`.
- Attacker-controlled HTML or module source is processed by Happy DOM.
- This may affect SSR, preview, scraping, or testing services that evaluate externally supplied HTML.

## Technical details

In `packages/happy-dom/src/module/ECMAScriptModuleCompiler.ts`, the named import handler splits an import specifier and extracts its alias:

```ts
const nameParts = part.trim().split(/\s+as\s+/);
const alias = (nameParts[1] || nameParts[0]).replace(/["']/g, '');
const name = nameParts[0].replace(/["']/g, '');

if (alias && name) {
  properties.push({ name, alias });
}
```

Unlike the patched `export { ... }` handler, the value of `alias` is not validated as a JavaScript identifier.

It is subsequently inserted directly into generated binding syntax:

```ts
newCodeStart += `let {${properties
  .map((property) =>
    property.alias
      ? `"${property.name}": ${property.alias}`
      : property.name
  )
  .join(', ')}} = $happy_dom.imports.get('${url}')${match[8]}`;
```

Consider the following source:

```js
import {
  missing as injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337
} from './dep.json' with { type: 'json' };
```

This is invalid ECMAScript module syntax. Node.js rejects it at the `=` token.

Happy DOM instead transforms it into the equivalent of:

```js
let {
  "missing": injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337
} = $happy_dom.imports.get('https://poc.local/dep.json');
```

This generated JavaScript is valid. Because the imported JSON object does not contain a `missing` property, the default initializer executes.

The `with { type: 'json' }` attribute is relevant because the compiler only generates its circular import resolver for ESM imports:

```ts
if (!match[7] || match[7] === 'esm') {
  resolvableCircularImports.push({ url, properties });
}
```

Using a JSON module prevents the malicious alias from being emitted again in a later circular-import assignment, leaving the generated function syntactically valid.

Backtick strings also survive the existing quote removal. This allows the injected initializer to reach Node.js host APIs:

```js
globalThis.constructor.constructor(`return process`)()
  .getBuiltinModule(`node:fs`)
  .mkdirSync(
    globalThis.constructor.constructor(`return process`)().cwd() +
      `/HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF`
  )
```

  "private": true,

items.title: Wasmtime: Panic lowering a host-created component model stream into a guest that expects a different payload type
items.summary:
### Summary

Wasmtime may panic when the host lowers a component model `stream` or `future` into a guest, if the host created that stream or future with one payload type and the guest expects a different one. This can happen when an embedder creates a stream or future, passes it through a guest, receives it back under a type-erased type such as `StreamAny` or `FutureAny`, and then passes it to a guest function with a different payload type.

GHSA-63h4-6cx9-pjfj is a related advisory also fixing issues within this area, and this advisory is being issued for portions of Wasmtime that were not fixed as part of that advisory.

### Impact

This affects embedders that do all of the following:

1. Create streams or futures on the host with `StreamReader::new` or `FutureReader::new`
2. Pass them to guest code and receive them back as `StreamAny`, `FutureAny`, `Val::Stream`/`Val::Future`, or a typed reader whose payload is one of these.
3. Pass them on to a guest function whose `stream` or `future` payload type differs from the type the host created them with.

A guest can cause the mismatch in step 3 when it controls the types of the functions it exports or of the values it returns. In that case a malicious guest can make the host panic, a denial of service. Embedders that only use statically typed `StreamReader<T>`/`FutureReader<T>` with concrete payload types throughout, or that never pass streams or futures they created through a guest and back, are not affected.

items.title: filelock ReadWriteLock: SQLite reopens the lock database by name, so a planted symlink or journal file makes the lock user's process overwrite or unlink its own files
items.summary:
`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.

Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J` [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H` scores 7.1 (High).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.

Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`.

items.title: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding leads to code execution
items.summary:
### Credits

**Researcher**: Alex Bouffard (mixbo@pebwalker.com)

### Summary

A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's FlashPix (FPX) JPEG-tile decoder lets an attacker achieve arbitrary code execution by getting an application to open a single crafted file with `Image.open()`. The file is recognized by content (the OLE2 magic), not by extension, so any service that opens or thumbnails untrusted uploads with the optional `olefile` dependency installed is reachable with no user interaction. In the PoC below, opening one crafted file executes an attacker-chosen command on stock Pillow 12.2.0 (x86_64 Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39).

### Details

`FpxImagePlugin` decodes FlashPix (FPX) files, which are OLE2/CFBF compound documents.

`Image.open()` auto-detects them from the OLE2 magic `D0CF11E0...` whenever the optional `olefile` package is installed (Pillow's documented dependency for FPX/MIC support), regardless of the file's extension.

For a JPEG-compressed subimage (`compression == 2`), the plugin builds a `"jpeg"` decode tile and derives the `(rawmode, jpegmode)` pair from attacker-controlled FPX color IDs through the `MODES` table ([`src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py` L25-L32](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py#L25-L32)):

```python
MODES = {
    ...
    (0x00018000, 0x00017FFE): ("RGBA", "LA"),                # rawmode "LA"  (2 bytes/pixel)
    ...
    (0x00020000, 0x00020001, 0x00020002): ("RGB", "YCC;P"),  # rawmode "YCC;P"
}
```

The Imaging output buffer for the tile is sized for the rawmode (here `"LA"` = 2 bytes/pixel) ([`src/decode.c` L223-L226](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/decode.c#L223-L226)):

```c
state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8;   // "LA" gives 2 * xsize bytes/row
...
state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes);
```

In `JpegDecode.c` the rawmode string is mapped to a libjpeg `out_color_space`. Recognized modes (`CMYK`, `YCbCr`, `YCbCrK`, and so on) get a concrete colorspace, but `"LA"` and `"YCC;P"` are not recognized, so control reaches the fallback branch ([`src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c` L219-L221](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c#L219-L221)):

```c
/* Disable decoder conversions. */
context->cinfo.jpeg_color_space = JCS_UNKNOWN;
context->cinfo.out_color_space  = JCS_UNKNOWN;
```

Under `JCS_UNKNOWN`, libjpeg performs no color conversion and emits `cinfo.num_components` bytes per pixel, taken from the embedded JPEG's SOF marker, which the attacker sets to 4. So `jpeg_read_scanlines` writes `4 * width` bytes per row into a buffer allocated for only `2 * width` bytes ([`src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c` L252](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c#L252)):

```c
ok = jpeg_read_scanlines(&context->cinfo, &state->buffer, 1);   // writes 4*W into a 2*W buffer
```

This is a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled length (the image width, up to tens of thousands of pixels, so about `2 * width` bytes of overflow per row) and attacker-controlled content (the decoded pixel data). The PoC weaponizes it: the overflow overwrites an adjacent Python `bytes` object's `ob_type` with a pointer to a fake `PyTypeObject` / `PyBufferProcs` vtable that the same overflow plants inside the decode buffer. When Pillow releases the input buffer, `PyBuffer_Release` walks `ob_type -> tp_as_buffer -> bf_releasebuffer` and executes `call *rax`; the PoC points that at `system@plt` (fixed, the interpreter binary is non-PIE) with `rdi` set to the command string, yielding command execution.

items.title: Pillow: Arrow export leaks stale heap memory when PILLOW_ALIGNMENT > 1
items.summary:
### Summary

When [`PILLOW_ALIGNMENT`](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/block_allocator.html#memory-pools) is set above 1, exporting an image to Arrow returns uninitialized heap memory mixed in with the pixel data. That memory can include pixels from images the process freed earlier. 

### Details

With an alignment above 1, the default allocator pads each row up to `aligned_linesize` and starts the first row at an aligned offset into the block. It then exports `im->blocks[0].ptr` as `xsize * ysize` tightly packed pixels, so exported data includes the padding bytes, and can include a few bytes from before the first row.

Tested vulnerable on 11.2.1, 12.3.0, 4c1ed27a5.

### PoC

Whether things leak may depend on allocator configuration. This does show a leak on my Mac.

```python
import os

os.environ["PILLOW_ALIGNMENT"] = "64"

from PIL import Image

# Image A: 64 px wide, so its rows fill the whole aligned stride
a = Image.new("L", (64, 40), 0x41).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)
del a

# Image B: 61 px wide, so each row has 3 bytes of padding; its pixels are all 0
b = Image.new("L", (61, 40), 0).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)

try:
    exported = Image.fromarrow(b, b.mode, b.size).tobytes()
except ValueError as e:
    print("Not vulnerable:", e)
else:
    if leaked := len(exported) - exported.count(0):
        raise RuntimeError(f"{leaked} of {len(exported)} exported bytes are not B's pixels")
```

### Impact

Information disclosure for applications that set `PILLOW_ALIGNMENT` and export images to Arrow. Likely any image whose row length isn't a multiple of the alignment will do. In a service handling several users' images, one user's exported data can contain pixels from another user's image, or other stale heap contents.

A user with only read access could cause irreversible data loss (e.g., a related table being emptied), without needing any write permissions. This could result in denial of service and loss of data integrity for affected applications.

items.title: fast-uri vulnerable to URI scheme spoofing via percent-encoded scheme decoding
items.summary:
### Impact

`fast-uri` percent-decodes the scheme component with the legacy global `unescape()` before validating it, so an input whose decoded scheme is a valid but dangerous token is emitted as a live scheme. RFC 3986 section 3.1 does not allow percent-encoding in a scheme, so no RFC or WHATWG parser treats such input as having that scheme, but `fast-uri` does.

For example, `normalize('%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, `resolve('https://a.example/', '%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, and `parse('%6Aavascript:alert(1)').scheme` returns `javascript`. The `%uXXXX` form (`%u006Aavascript:`) produces the same result, and `equal('%68ttp://a/', 'http://a/')` returns `true`.

An application that screens dangerous schemes on the raw input and then stores or renders `normalize(input)` or `resolve(base, input)` turns an inert string into an executable `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` URL, a stored or reflected cross-site scripting vector in the consuming application. `equal()` also treats an encoded and a plain scheme as the same, which can bypass equality-based allowlists.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Reject input whose scheme part (before the first `:`, and before any `/`, `?`, or `#`) contains `%`. Alternatively, check `parse(x).scheme` against an allowlist after normalization and use that same parsed result rather than the raw string.

items.title: fast-uri vulnerable to improper path equivalence in relative reference normalization
items.summary:
### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `normalize()` and `serialize()` apply RFC 3986 dot-segment removal (`remove_dot_segments`) to the path of a relative-path reference. RFC 3986 section 5.2.4 defines that algorithm only for the merged target path during resolution, not for the reference itself, so applied to the reference it drops leading `..` segments and can turn a document-relative reference into a root-relative one.

For example, `normalize('a/../b')` returns `/b` and `normalize('../x')` returns `x`, so `resolve(base, normalize(ref))` points at a different resource than `resolve(base, ref)`, and `equal()` treats distinct references as the same.

Applications that normalize attacker-supplied or user-supplied relative references and then resolve them, or use them as cache, deduplication, or authorization keys, can have a reference escape its intended directory and point at a different resource.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Do not normalize a relative reference before resolving it. Resolve it against the absolute base first, then normalize the absolute result.

items.title: fast-uri vulnerable to host confusion via unchecked WHATWG host canonicalization
items.summary:
### Impact

`fast-uri` versions `>= 2.4.2, <= 2.4.7`, `>= 3.1.3, <= 3.1.8`, and `>= 4.0.1, <= 4.2.2` can silently rewrite the host of an HTTP-family URL (`http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`, or any scheme with `domainHost: true`). For those schemes `canonicalizeHost()` passes the parsed host to the WHATWG `URL` parser and adopts its `.hostname` without checking that the parser read the whole input as a host. RFC 3986 permits `@` inside the host group and the WHATWG parser strips TAB, LF, and CR, so the authority `fast-uri` reports is rewritten by that second parser with no `error` set: data before an `@` is dropped and whitespace is removed.

For example, `fast-uri` parses `http://a@b@evil.example/` to host `evil.example` (dropping the `b` segment), and a host containing a raw TAB, CR, or LF has those characters stripped. `equal()` then treats a whitespace-smuggled host as the same as the clean one, and `resolve()` rewrites the authority the same way.

Applications that use `fast-uri` to enforce host-based policy (denylists, loopback filtering, redirect validation, outbound proxy routing) on one representation, such as the raw input, see a policy/use desync: the canonical host `fast-uri` returns differs from what was checked, and traffic can be steered to an unintended destination.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Reject URIs whose authority contains more than one `@`, or contains TAB, CR, or LF, before calling `fast-uri`. Alternatively, treat any non-empty `parse(x).error` as fatal, and compare hosts only from the same `parse()` result.

items.title: fast-uri vulnerable to scheme injection via an unescaped first-segment colon in suffix references
items.summary:
### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `serialize()`, `normalize()`, and `resolve()`, when called with the non-default option `reference: 'suffix'` on a reference that has no authority, emit a relative reference whose first path segment contains a bare colon without escaping it. RFC 3986 section 3.3 requires the first segment of a `path-noscheme` reference not to contain a colon, precisely because a bare colon makes the string reparse as an absolute URI with a scheme. `fast-uri`'s default serialization escapes that colon, but the suffix path does not.

For example, `normalize('javascript:alert(1)', { reference: 'suffix' })` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, which reparses as a live `javascript:` scheme; `data:` and `vbscript:` behave the same.

Applications that serialize or normalize a relative reference with `reference: 'suffix'` and then treat the result as a URI can turn inert input into a live `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` URL (a cross-site scripting vector), and `equal()` can conflate a scheme-bearing reference with a relative one. Exposure is limited to applications that use the non-default `reference: 'suffix'` option.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Do not use the `reference: 'suffix'` option on untrusted input. If suffix output is required, percent-encode a colon in the first path segment of the result before treating it as a URI.

items.title: HTTP::Headers::ActionPack versions before 0.10 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via Accept-Language...
items.summary:
HTTP::Headers::ActionPack versions before 0.10 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via Accept-Language ranges matched as regular expressions.

_language_match interpolates each Accept-Language range into the pattern `/^$range\-/i` without escaping it, so regular expression syntax in the header reaches the regex engine. A 12-byte range such as `(a?|b?){26}z` backtracks for seconds, and each increment of the quantifier doubles the time. An invalid range such as `(` fails to compile.

A remote attacker can exhaust CPU, or make choose_language die, in any application that passes an untrusted Accept-Language header to it.

items.title: SvelteKit: URL redirection to untrusted site via enhanced form submission
items.summary:
### Impact
Applications using enhanced form actions (`use:enhance`) on routes that accept paths beginning with `//`, such as catch-all routes, may be vulnerable to an open redirect.

### Patches
A fix has been prepared for `@sveltejs/kit` 3.0.0. Users should upgrade to 3.0.0 or later.

The fix preserves leading double slashes in action paths without generating protocol-relative URLs, restricts non-redirect action navigation to the current origin, and includes the origin when comparing action locations with the current page.

### Workarounds
Reject requests whose parsed URL pathname begins with `//` before route resolution, for example in a reverse proxy or a SvelteKit `handle` hook.

Alternatively, disable navigation for non-redirect enhanced form results by supplying a custom submission callback:

```svelte
<form method="POST" use:enhance={() => ({ update }) => update({ navigate: false })}>
  <!-- form fields -->
</form>
```

This applies non-redirect results to the current page instead of navigating to the action location.

items.title: Tokio: Race condition in `tokio::time::Interval`
items.summary:
### Summary

On the multi-threaded runtime, there is a race condition between `Interval::poll_tick` and the runtime's time driver.

This affects `Interval` only. `Sleep` and `Timeout` are **not** affected.

### Details

In Tokio v1.54.0, a race condition between `tokio::time::Interval::poll_tick` (including `.tick().await`) and the runtime time driver can drop an internal timer entry without synchronizing with the driver thread that is firing it. This causes a data race and use-after-free on the timer's waker and task state in safe Rust, leading to assertion panics, task reference-count corruption, or heap memory corruption.

This bug was introduced by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8458, and it was fixed by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8692.

### Impact

This may lead to crashes and use-after-frees in applications using `Interval` on a multi-threaded runtime.

Since this issue is known to lead to crashes in production systems, the v1.54.0 release of Tokio has been yanked.

### Credits

Thank you to [creepycode](https://github.com/ByteZ1337) and [carabistouille](https://github.com/carabistouflette) for reporting this privately using the procedure outlined in our security policy. They both reported the issue independently of each other.

items.title: body-parser vulnerable to Denial of Service via trailing bytes after a compressed request body
items.summary:
### Impact

A single request can crash any application using `body-parser` with default options. When a request carries a `Content-Encoding` (for example `gzip`), `body-parser` pipes it into a decompression stream and, after reading the body, leaves that stream piped with no error listener. A payload of one valid compressed frame followed by trailing bytes decodes and the application responds normally, but the trailing bytes then reach the already-finished decoder, which emits an error that is re-thrown as an uncaught exception and terminates the process. No authentication or matching route is required, since parsing runs before routing.

### Patches

Fixed in body-parser 2.4.0 and 1.20.9. Upgrade to one of these versions.

### Workarounds

Pass `inflate: false` to the body-parser middleware if the application does not need to accept compressed request bodies. This rejects encoded requests before any decompression stream is created.

items.title: Strands Agents SDK: Exposure of data element to wrong session in the A2A Server
items.summary:
**Summary**  
Strands Agents SDK is an open-source SDK, available for Python (strands-agents) and TypeScript (@strands-agents/sdk), for building and running AI agents. An issue exists where, under certain circumstances, the Agent2Agent (A2A) server shares conversation history across callers with different context\_id values, allowing one caller to read and influence another caller's session.  
  
**Impact**  
The A2A server did not properly isolate conversation state between callers. In multi-tenant deployments, an authenticated remote user could access another caller's conversation history or influence model behavior for other callers (CWE-488: Unintended Disclosure of Data Element to Wrong Session). This affects any deployment where an A2A server is reachable by more than one user or tenant.  
  
**Impacted versions:**  
strands-agents (Python): all versions containing the multiagent.a2a module, < 1.43.0  
@strands-agents/sdk (TypeScript): < 1.5.0  
  
**Patches**  
This issue has been addressed in strands-agents version 1.43.0 and @strands-agents/sdk version 1.5.0. The A2A server now uses an agent factory so conversation state is isolated per A2A context\_id. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.  
  
**Workarounds**  
There is no workaround that fully addresses this issue in affected versions. Until you upgrade, do not expose an A2A server to more than one user or tenant. If multiple callers need access, run a separate A2A server instance for each user or tenant.  
  
**References**  
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, we ask that you contact AWS Security via our [vulnerability reporting page](https://aws.amazon.com/security/vulnerability-reporting) or directly via email to [aws-security@amazon.com](mailto:aws-security@amazon.com). Please do not create a public GitHub issue.

items.title: virtualenv: Bash activator leaves the --prompt value unescaped in PS1 when promptvars is off, so prompt expansion later executes it (regression in 21.14.9)
items.summary:
## Summary

The bash activator puts the caller-supplied prompt value into `PS1` unescaped whenever `promptvars` is off at activation time, and assumes prompt expansion can never run afterwards. `promptvars` and posix mode are runtime shell state, not a property of the activation moment: re-enabling prompt expansion in the same shell (`shopt -s promptvars`, `set -o posix`) or starting an interactive child bash that inherits the exported `PS1` makes bash expand the stored value and run the command substitution in it. An attacker who controls the prompt value gets command execution as the user who sources `bin/activate`.

This is a regression. 21.14.8 escaped `$` and the backtick unconditionally and stays inert under the same sequence. The 21.14.9 fix for GHSA-6w3r-xr62-4xcp (#3418) rewrote that block and left bash with a path that stores the raw value whenever `promptvars` is off.

## Affected area

Activation scripts (activate, activate.bat, activate.csh, activate.fish, activate.nu, Activate.ps1, activate.xsh) — specifically the bash `bin/activate`.

## Attacker-controlled input

The `--prompt` value, which the security policy already lists as a value that may come from project metadata the user did not write. It reaches `virtualenv` as `--prompt` on the command line or as the `prompt` argument of the API, is written into `bin/activate` as the literal `VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT` assignment (correctly quoted, the value arrives there as data), and the script then copies it into `PS1` without escaping `$` or the backtick.

Example: a repository or tool config supplies a prompt such as `x$(id > /tmp/ve-pwn)y`; the victim creates and later activates the environment.

## Details

Source of the latest release: [`src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh` lines 140-160](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/21.14.12/src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh#L140-L160)

```sh
if [ -z "${VIRTUAL_ENV_DISABLE_PROMPT-}" ] &&
    { [ -n "${BASH_VERSION-}" ] || [ -n "${ZSH_VERSION-}" ]; }; then
    _OLD_VIRTUAL_PS1="${PS1-}"
    # bash expands PS1 after decoding its prompt escapes when promptvars is on or in posix mode, so the prompt holds a
    # reference to the variable and its value never reaches that expansion; otherwise only the decode runs and
    # backslashes need doubling. ...
    if [ -n "${BASH_VERSION-}" ] && { shopt -q promptvars || shopt -qo posix; }; then
        PS1='(${VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT-}) '"${PS1-}"
    else
        _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT//\\/\\\\}"
        if [ -n "${ZSH_VERSION-}" ]; then
            _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT//\$/\\\$}"
            _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT//\`/\\\`}"
            _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT//\%/%%}"
        fi
        PS1="(${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT}) ${PS1-}"
        unset _VIRTUAL_PROMPT
    fi
fi
```

Two separate mistakes combine:

1. A runtime shell option is treated as a constant. `shopt -u promptvars` at the moment of `source` does not bind the shell forever: `shopt -s promptvars` and `set -o posix` both re-enable PS1 expansion in the same shell. The code itself tests `shopt -qo posix` because posix mode expands the prompt regardless of `promptvars`, which shows the expansion state is not fixed by the activation.
2. The escaping that would keep the value inert in that mode is missing for bash. GHSA-5vjq-rrrf-7h2q ("activate runs commands from the environment name in zsh with PROMPT_SUBST") fixed exactly this shape for zsh, reasoning that "a user can set it after activation", by escaping `$` and the backtick. Bash lost the equivalent escaping in the same commit that added the zsh branch.

The rendered prompt shows the regression directly:

```
21.14.8   PS1 = (x\\$(id > /tmp/ve-pwn)y)       <- escaped, inert
21.14.9   PS1 = (x$(id > /tmp/ve-pwn)y)         <- raw value
21.14.12  PS1 = (x$(id > /tmp/ve-pwn)y)         <- raw value
```

Relevant commit: [`5f48d711` "fix(bash): preserve literal prompts in supported shells (#3418)"](https://github.com/pypa/vi

items.summary:
The Include directive in `src/mistune/directives/include.py` does not validate that the resolved file path stays within the source directory, allowing path traversal via `../` sequences to read arbitrary files.

Additionally, error messages and included file contents are rendered without HTML escaping, leading to XSS even when `escape=True`.

Affected functions:
- Path resolution (lines 27-31)
- `block_error()` in html.py (line 140)
- `render_html_include()` (line 72)

The Include plugin must be explicitly enabled via the plugins parameter.
