items.title: Twisted: Denial of Service in the Twisted IMAP4 Server via a Negative Literal Size in SEARCH
items.summary:
## Summary

An infinite-loop vulnerability (CWE-835) in the Twisted IMAP4 server lets an authenticated client freeze the whole process with one small command. `twisted.mail.imap4.parseNestedParens` reads an IMAP literal size with `int()` and never rejects a negative value. A negative size such as `{-100}` drives the parser cursor negative, and because a negative Python index wraps around the end of the string instead of raising, the scanning loop never terminates. It runs synchronously on the single-threaded reactor, so one `SEARCH` command holds the reactor at full CPU forever and every other connection stops being served.

## Details

Meeting an inline literal, `parseNestedParens` reads the size between the braces and advances the cursor past the body:

```python
# twisted/mail/imap4.py  parseNestedParens
literalSize = int(s[i + 1 : end])          # no sign check
contentStack[-1].append((s[end + 3 : end + 3 + literalSize],))
i = end + 3 + literalSize                    # negative size -> i goes negative
```

`int(b"-100")` is `-100`, so `i` goes negative; the loop condition `i < len(s)` stays true and `s[i : i + 1]` on a negative index never raises, so the cursor cycles forever. The `_literalStringLimit` guard only covers the synchronizing-literal continuation path, not this inline branch. The call is reached from `select_SEARCH` through `arg_searchkeys`, dispatched only in the selected state, so a valid login and a selected mailbox (any low-privilege account) suffice. It runs in the reactor thread, and the connection timeout cannot fire because the reactor itself is frozen.

Affected product: Twisted (`twisted.mail`), the IMAP4 server `twisted.mail.imap4.IMAP4Server`
Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier

## PoC

Log in, select a mailbox, and send a `SEARCH` whose literal size is negative:

```text
C: t1 LOGIN testuser password-test
C: t2 SELECT INBOX
C: t3 SEARCH {-100}zzzzzzzzzz
```

The server never responds and one core stays at 100 percent. In a measured run a health service co-hosted on the same reactor stopped answering the instant the command arrived, showing the freeze hits the whole process and not just the attacking connection. A valid `{5}zzzzz` completes normally and a non-numeric `{abc}` is rejected with a parse error, which isolates the cause to the missing negative-size check.

## Impact

A remote denial of service. One command of about ten bytes freezes the single-threaded reactor, so it stops serving not only every other IMAP connection but every other service co-hosted in the same process (for example SMTP and POP3 under `twistd mail`), and no timeout can recover it until the process is restarted. It requires an authenticated session, so any account holder can trigger it; there is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution.

items.title: Twisted: Unauthenticated Remote Denial of Service in the Twisted IRC Server via an Unbounded Line Buffer
items.summary:
## Summary

An unbounded-buffer vulnerability (CWE-770) in the Twisted words IRC server lets any unauthenticated remote client exhaust server memory. `twisted.words.protocols.irc.IRC.dataReceived` appends every received byte to a per-connection buffer and only removes data at a line feed, with no maximum length. Because `IRC` is a plain `Protocol` and not a `LineReceiver`, one connection that streams bytes without a line feed grows the buffer without bound and drives the whole single-threaded process to out-of-memory, dropping every user at once. The `twistd words` server inherits the method unchanged through `IRCUser`, and the data is buffered before any authentication.

## Details

`IRC.dataReceived` keeps everything up to the last line feed in `self.buffer`:

```python
# twisted/words/protocols/irc.py
class IRC(protocol.Protocol):        # not a LineReceiver, so no MAX_LENGTH
    buffer = ""
    def dataReceived(self, data):
        if isinstance(data, bytes):
            data = data.decode("utf-8")
        lines = (self.buffer + data).split(LF)
        self.buffer = lines.pop()    # no 3line feed -> whole input stays buffered
        ...
```

With no line feed in the data, `lines.pop()` returns the entire accumulated content to `self.buffer`, so it grows by every chunk and is never bounded; `IRC` defines no `MAX_LENGTH`, no `lineLengthExceeded`, and no timeout, so the connection is never closed. The `twistd words` server protocol `IRCUser` subclasses `IRC` without overriding `dataReceived`, and the buffer is filled before any `PASS`, `NICK`, or `USER`, so no credentials are required.

Affected product: Twisted (`twisted.words`), `twisted.words.protocols.irc.IRC` and its subclass `twisted.words.service.IRCUser`
Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier

## PoC

On a standard Twisted words IRC server (the server `twistd words` runs, using `IRCUser`), an unauthenticated client opens a single TCP connection and continuously sends data that contains no line feed, never completing a line. Every chunk is appended to the connection's line buffer, and because no complete line is ever formed none of it is consumed, so the buffer grows by the full volume sent.

In a measured run against a real `IRCFactory` server, one unauthenticated connection sending 60 MB of line-feed-free data raised the server process resident memory from about 47 MB to 2966 MB (roughly 49 MB per MB sent) with the connection still open and no limit triggered. Sending the same volume as normal line-feed-terminated commands leaves memory flat, which isolates the cause to the missing line-length bound.

## Impact

An unauthenticated remote denial of service from allocation without limits (CWE-770) leading to uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400). A single credential-free connection exhausts the memory of the whole `twistd words` process, and because one process serves every user, the crash drops all connections at once and the service stays down until it is restarted. The quadratic buffer copy reaches the same effect faster. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution.

items.title: Twisted: Unauthenticated Remote Denial of Service in the Twisted conch Telnet Transport via an Unbounded Subnegotiation Buffer
items.summary:
## Summary

An allocation-without-limits vulnerability (CWE-770) in the Twisted conch telnet transport lets any unauthenticated remote peer exhaust server memory over a single connection. When the peer opens a telnet subnegotiation with `IAC SB` and then streams bytes without ever sending the `IAC SE` terminator, every byte is appended to a per-connection buffer that has no maximum length. The buffer persists across reads and is released only on the terminator the attacker withholds, so it grows without bound until the process is killed.

## Details

The option-negotiation state machine in `Telnet.dataReceived` enters the `subnegotiation` state on `IAC SB` and sets an empty command list. In that state every non-`IAC` byte is appended to the list with no length check:

```python
# src/twisted/conch/telnet.py  (Telnet.dataReceived)
elif self.state == "subnegotiation":
    if b == IAC:
        self.state = "subnegotiation-escaped"
    else:
        self.commands.append(b)      # unbounded: no len(self.commands) check
```

`self.commands` is an instance attribute that persists across `dataReceived` calls and is deleted only when `IAC SE` completes the subnegotiation. Negotiation runs at the transport layer before authentication, and the bytes are consumed inside `dataReceived` before any application callback, so an application cannot impose a bound. Twisted caps other parser buffers, for example `NetstringReceiver.MAX_LENGTH`, but not this one.

Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.conch.telnet` transport
Affected versions: confirmed against 26.4.0

## PoC

On any endpoint that exposes the Twisted telnet transport, such as the Twisted manhole telnet service, open one connection and send the two bytes `IAC SB` (`0xFF 0xFA`), then stream any non-`0xFF` bytes continuously and never send the `IAC SE` terminator (`0xFF 0xF0`). No credentials are required, because option negotiation runs before authentication.

Every byte is appended to the per-connection subnegotiation buffer with no maximum, and the buffer is released only by the terminator the attacker withholds, so it grows for the life of the connection. Because each byte is retained as a separate element the memory consumed is several times the traffic sent, so a modest-bandwidth peer, or several such connections, drives the process to memory exhaustion.

## Impact

This is an unauthenticated remote denial of service (CWE-770, CWE-400) by memory exhaustion. A single connection grows an in-memory buffer without bound at a cost proportional to the bytes sent, amplified by per-byte object overhead, until the operating system kills the server and every service it hosts. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution. The affected surface is any deployment that exposes a Twisted telnet or manhole transport to untrusted peers.

items.title: Twisted: Unauthenticated Remote Denial of Service in the Twisted words domish XML Element Stream via an Unbounded Element Tree
items.summary:
## Summary

An allocation-without-limits vulnerability in the Twisted XML element stream lets any unauthenticated remote peer exhaust server memory over a single stream. When the peer opens a container element and streams child elements without ever closing the container, every element is materialised into an in-memory tree with no limit on depth or child count. An element is released only when its end tag arrives, so a container the attacker never closes retains everything beneath it until the process is killed.

## Details

In `ExpatElementStream._onStartElement`, each start tag appends a new element to the current element's children and descends into it, with no depth or child-count check:

```python
# src/twisted/words/xish/domish.py  (ExpatElementStream._onStartElement)
if self.documentStarted == 1:
    if self.currElem != None:
        self.currElem.children.append(e)   # append child: no depth/count cap
        e.parent = self.currElem
    self.currElem = e                      # descend into the new element
```

An element is emitted and dropped only when its end tag arrives while it sits directly under the document root, so a container that is never closed keeps every child beneath it. The transport `XmlStream.dataReceived` feeds bytes to `self.stream.parse(data)` with no size limit, and in XMPP the stream is parsed during negotiation before authentication.

Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.words.xish.domish` element stream
Affected versions: confirmed against 26.4.0

## PoC

On any endpoint that parses untrusted XML streams with this stack, such as an XMPP server, open a stream by sending the opening `stream:stream` tag and a container element, then stream child elements continuously and never send the container's closing tag. No credentials are required, because in XMPP the stream is parsed before authentication.

Every child is appended to the container and retained because the container is never emitted, and the transport applies no limit on the size of the unfinished document. Because each small element becomes a full object in memory the footprint is many times the traffic sent, so a modest-bandwidth peer, or several such streams, drives the process to memory exhaustion.

## Impact

This is an unauthenticated remote denial of service by memory exhaustion. A single stream grows an in-memory element tree without bound, amplified by per-element object overhead, until the operating system kills the server. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution. The affected surface is any deployment that parses untrusted XML streams with this stack, such as an XMPP server or component.

items.title: Twisted: HTTP Request Smuggling in twisted.web via a Bare CR or LF in a Header Value
items.summary:
## Summary

An incomplete header-value validation (CWE-444) in the Twisted HTTP server lets a bare carriage return or line feed in a header value hide a following header from the parser. `twisted.web.http.HTTPChannel.headerReceived` rejects a NUL byte in a header value but not a bare CR or LF, even though RFC 9110 section 5.5 requires a recipient to reject all three. Because the channel splits requests only on CRLF, a value carrying a bare LF and a second header arrives as one line, so the second header is folded into the value and the request is framed with no body. A front-end that treats the bare LF as a line terminator frames the request differently, and the disagreement lets an attacker smuggle a request past it. This is an incomplete fix of the earlier Twisted request-smuggling advisories, which guarded the NUL sibling of this exact check.

## Details

`headerReceived` splits a header line on the first colon, strips space and tab from the value, and validates it with a single test that rejects only NUL:

```python
# twisted/web/http.py  HTTPChannel.headerReceived
data = data.strip(b" \t")
if b"\x00" in data:          # NUL rejected; a bare CR or LF is not
    self._respondToBadRequestAndDisconnect()
    return False
```

The channel delimiter is CRLF, so `Foo: x\nContent-Length: 39` is one line: the split yields name `Foo` and value `x\nContent-Length: 39`, `strip` leaves the LF, and the NUL check passes. `_maybeChooseTransferDecoder` is then called with `Foo`, never sees a `Content-Length`, and installs no body decoder, so the request is framed with an empty body. The header name and request line already reject CR and LF, so the value is the only gap.

Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.web.http.HTTPChannel`
Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier

## PoC

Feed one connection a request whose header value carries a bare LF and a `Content-Length`, followed by a second request in the bytes after it: `POST /public HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: v\r\nFoo: x\nContent-Length: 44\r\n\r\nGET /admin HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: internal\r\n\r\n`. Twisted parses two requests and serves both, so the smuggled `GET /admin` returns the /admin response body even though the visible request was only `POST /public`. The bare CR variant behaves identically, and a NUL in the value is rejected, which isolates the missing CR and LF checks.

Behind a front-end that treats the bare LF as a line terminator, the front-end frames one `POST /public` and forwards a body while Twisted frames a second `GET /admin`; the extra response then poisons the shared connection, so a later victim receives the attacker's `GET /admin` response.

## Impact

This is an HTTP request-smuggling exposure (CWE-444) from inconsistent interpretation of a request (CWE-436). Through a front-end that accepts a bare CR or LF as a line terminator, an attacker can smuggle a request the front-end never sees, bypassing front-end access controls, poisoning a shared connection so a later victim receives the attacker's response, and poisoning a cache. Twisted is the strict endpoint that frames the request without a body, so it is realized only behind such a proxy, and there is no code execution.

items.title: SvelteKit : XSS via untrusted cache-control header in prerendered page
items.summary:
### Impact

Applications that prerender pages and use `setHeaders` to set a `cache-control` header from an untrusted source are vulnerable to cross-site scripting (XSS).

SvelteKit inserts the header value into a `<meta http-equiv="cache-control">` tag without escaping it. An attacker who can influence this value at prerender time can break out of the `content` attribute and inject HTML or JavaScript into the generated page. The injected code can then execute when users visit the page.

### Patches

The fix escapes the header value before inserting it into the generated HTML. Upgrade to `@sveltejs/kit` version 3.0.0 or later.

### Workarounds

Avoid forwarding untrusted `cache-control` header values with `setHeaders` on prerendered pages. Use a fixed, trusted cache policy instead.

items.title: obsidian-tc: Memory-lifecycle tools overwrite unowned notes or partially commit lifecycle changes
items.summary:
### Summary
`create_entity`, `link_entities`, `rename_entity`, `unlink_entities` and `delete_entity` regenerate a memory note's body from SQLite at the computed `memory/<type>/<name>.md` path. When a note already existed at that path and was not owned by the entity being written (a hand-authored note, or an orphan left by a different entity whose name sanitized to the same path), its entire body was overwritten on the next write naming that `(type, name)`, keeping only its frontmatter. Separately, several of these tools inserted or removed their SQLite row before the fallible filesystem step, so a refused note write could leave a relation gone, a retired status committed, or the wrong entity deleted.

### Details
- `create_entity` and `link_entities` inserted the SQL row or relation before materialization.
- `rename_entity` seeded the destination path with a direct atomic write that bypassed the ownership check, and for a status-only rename could commit a retired status with the note write refused.
- `unlink_entities` removed the relation row before discovering the source note's rematerialization would be refused.
- `delete_entity`'s cascade could delete the target and its relations before a neighbour's note was found to be foreign.

The overwrite exists in every released version since `materializeEntity` shipped (`git show v1.0.1:packages/server/src/memory/materialize.ts`).

### Impact
An authorized caller with memory-write scope (any agent using the M5 memory tools) can, without intending to, destroy the body of a vault note outside the entity it is writing, and can leave the memory graph inconsistent with the notes on disk. Snapshots-before-write (`restore_note`) mitigate the overwrite only where snapshots are enabled and the note had been written through obsidian-tc before.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.31.4 at the shared primitive: `materializeEntity` refuses to write over a note whose `obsidian_tc_id` is missing or belongs to another entity; a new `assertNoteOwnership` pre-check runs before any SQLite mutation in the three lifecycle tools, so a refusal is a no-op; `create_entity` and `link_entities` roll back the row they had inserted. Verified by `test/m5-memory-ownership.test.ts`, which covers all five call sites and the rollback.

### Workarounds
None that preserve the tools. Disabling the `write:memory` scope for callers prevents the write path entirely.

### Credit
Found by the maintainer while building `obsidian-tc memory import` (PR #978); the vulnerability class was independently confirmed by a cross-vendor adversarial review.

### References
- PR #978 (fix and test), CHANGELOG `## [1.31.4] ### Security`
- `packages/server/src/memory/materialize.ts`, `packages/server/src/tools/m5/memory-lifecycle-tools.ts`

---

items.title: SiYuan: authFilePublishAccess distinguishes hidden and forbidden documents from public and nonexistent ones, and issues a publish-auth cookie for documents it reports as forbidden
items.summary:
### Summary

`/api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess` is registered with `CheckAuth` only and is reachable anonymously. It never sets a failure code, so its outcome is signalled entirely by the response message and by whether a `Set-Cookie` header is present. Those two signals differ across access tiers, which lets an anonymous caller determine, for any candidate document identifier, whether that document is public or nonexistent, password-protected, or exists at the hidden or forbidden tier.

Separately, hidden and forbidden entries carry an empty password. Submitting `password:""` therefore satisfies the equality check for them, and the server responds by issuing `Set-Cookie: publish-auth-<docID>` for a document whose own tier is forbidden.

### Details

**Route,** identical on both refs:

```go
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess", model.CheckAuth, authFilePublishAccess)
```

No `CheckAdminRole`, no `CheckReadonly`.

**Handler,** `kernel/api/filetree.go:1608` on the development branch and `:1421` on master. `ret.Code` is never assigned on the failure path, so every response carries `code:0`. The branch is:

```go
if item.Password == password {
    // SetPublishAuthCookie
} else {
    ret.Msg = Conf.Language(285)
}
```

**The cookie is issued for forbidden documents.** Entries at the hidden and forbidden tiers store `Password == ""`. A request with `password:""` therefore makes `item.Password == password` true for them, and the handler takes the success branch. The server issues a publish-auth cookie for a document it otherwise treats as inaccessible.

The cookie itself confers nothing, because those tiers are decided before any password check elsewhere in the codebase. The defect is that the endpoint's success signal does not correspond to access being granted, and that signal is observable.

**Three distinguishable outcomes.** With `password:""`, one request per candidate identifier:

| Tier of the target | `Set-Cookie` | Body |
|---|---|---|
| Public (no publish-access entry) | absent | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |
| Nonexistent identifier | absent | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |
| Password-protected | absent | `{"code":0,"msg":"Password is incorrect"}` |
| Hidden | **present** | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |
| Forbidden | **present** | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |

Public and nonexistent are indistinguishable from each other, which is correct. Everything else separates. A caller learns whether a given identifier names a password-protected document, or a document that exists at the hidden or forbidden tier, which is precisely the class the publish tiers exist to conceal.

**Identifiers are readily available.** Document and block identifiers appear in the DOM of published pages, in reference and backlink payloads, and in annotation reference data. The caller does not need to guess them.

**A fourth response on the development branch.** `IsEncryptedPublishRuntimeTarget` sets `ret.Code = -1`, which identifies the supplied identifier as belonging to an encrypted notebook. That is a membership oracle for encrypted notebooks, the same data class as `GHSA-f2rw-w22v-54vh`.

### Proof of Concept

Publish mode enabled, `Publish.Auth.Enable` false, anonymous client. One request per candidate identifier, all with an empty password:

```
POST /api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess
{"id":"<candidate document id>","password":""}
```

Comparing the response message and the presence of `Set-Cookie` against the table above classifies the identifier. Documents at the hidden and forbidden tiers return a publish-auth cookie and an empty message, distinguishing them both from public documents and from identifiers that name nothing at all.

An anonymous reader in publish mode, or any publish `RoleReader`, can classify arbitrary document identifiers by access tier and confirm the existence of documents at the hidden and forbidden tiers. items.summary:

As a result, code running under `--permission` with restricted `--allow-fs-read` can still use `fs.realpathSync()` to check file existence, resolve symlink targets, and enumerate filesystem paths outside of permitted directories.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**, **24.x**, and **22.x**.

items.title: A flaw in Node.js `crypto` causes the internal entropy caches used by `crypto.randomUUID()`, ...
items.summary:
A flaw in Node.js `crypto` causes the internal entropy caches used by `crypto.randomUUID()`, `crypto.randomUUIDv7()`, and `crypto.randomInt()` to be saved into user-land startup snapshots (`--build-snapshot`) and single executable applications built with `useSnapshot`.

If any of these functions, or an API that relies on them such as `URL.createObjectURL()`, is called while the snapshot is built, every process started from that snapshot returns the same values until the cache is refilled: up to 127 UUIDs and about 1,000 `randomInt()` values. Identifiers expected to be unique can collide across processes, and values issued by one process can be predicted by observing another.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**, **24.x**, and **22.x**.

items.title: A flaw in Node.js Permission Model filesystem enforcement can grant access to paths that do not...
items.summary:
A flaw in Node.js Permission Model filesystem enforcement can grant access to paths that do not match a wildcard `--allow-fs-read` or `--allow-fs-write` rule.

When the requested path is shorter than the prefix of a wildcard grant, the radix tree lookup stops comparing early and treats the path as a match. For example, `--allow-fs-read=/etc/passwd.*` also allows reading `/etc/passwd`. This requires the wildcard grant to sit directly under the root of the permission tree, for example when it is the only grant for that scope. This is a different root cause from CVE-2026-58043.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**.

items.title: A flaw was found in Kruize Autotune. Its REST API ships without an authentication layer, and the...
items.summary: A flaw was found in Kruize Autotune. Its REST API ships without an authentication layer, and the endpoints that return datasource configuration — the list-datasources endpoint (GET /datasources) and the datasource-metadata endpoint — serialized datasource objects using a default Gson configuration with no field-exclusion strategy. As a result, the authentication secrets stored for each configured monitoring datasource (basic-auth passwords, bearer tokens, API keys, and OAuth2 client secrets) were returned in cleartext to any client able to reach the service. An attacker with network access to Autotune could harvest these credentials and reuse them to authenticate to the backing monitoring stack.

items.title: The AI Agent Nobody Owns: Watch Expert Webinar On Your Newest Insider Threat
items.summary:
Right now, there is probably an AI agent running on a laptop somewhere in your network. It stores API keys and database passwords, can access your internal systems, and works without anyone watching.

Nobody reviewed its access. Nobody owns it.

If an employee had that much reach with that little oversight, you would call it an insider risk. So why do we still call the agent a productivity tool?

items.title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
items.summary: In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation. We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92). We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.

items.title: AgentPhishing: A Benchmark of LLM Email Agents Under Adaptive Attack
items.summary: Computer-use agents increasingly handle private information and act on users' behalf across desktop and web applications, including email. Phishing therefore poses privacy and security risks that depend not only on whether agents recognize malicious messages, but also on how they respond. Existing phishing datasets were developed primarily for conventional detection, leaving agent susceptibility to persuasive malicious requests insufficiently characterized. To expose vulnerabilities that pre-existing datasets may miss, we introduce AgentPhishing, a benchmark for evaluating whether persuasive phishing attacks can evade detection and induce LLM email agents to comply with malicious requests. We develop PhishOpt, which optimizes reusable email-generation skills against individual agents under fixed benchmark constraints and a realism constraint. We analyze the generated emails using Cialdini's persuasion principles to identify strategies associated with agent failures and use these findings to construct a universal generation skill. Our evaluation shows that agents can handle pre-existing phishing emails safely yet remain susceptible to attacks adapted to agent behavior, while in an AgentPhishing evaluation of nine agents, four exhibit phishing-detection rates below $10\%$ and malicious-request compliance rates above $45\%$. These results highlight the limits of inferring agent safety from conventional phishing evaluations and the need to assess how agents respond to persuasive malicious requests.

items.title: AfterDeleteBench: Auditing Post-Deletion Information Persistence in LLM Agents
items.summary: Many LLM agents maintain external persistent memory and derive additional state from past interactions, such as summaries. Deleting an original memory record therefore need not remove information carried by its descendants. We introduce AfterDeleteBench, a controlled behavioral audit for this failure mode in fixed-weight LLM agents. For each synthetic secret, we compare an exposed-then-deleted agent with an otherwise matched agent that was never exposed to the secret, allowing post-deletion recovery to be attributed to the original exposure. In our primary setting, a single query recovers the deleted secret from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while matched never-exposed controls have zero recovery. Crucially, recovery does not require a surviving verbatim copy: when the complete secret string is absent and only separately stored components remain under a public composition rule, exact reconstruction succeeds in 62-99% of cases across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3. We also show that the response interface is part of the measurement system: target-bearing replies can be scored as failures when the requested format and parser are misaligned. Finally, we separate reconstruction from write-back and fresh-session recall. Provenance-aware closure eliminates observed recovery in the tested positive-baseline settings, whereas an exact-literal write filter blocks reinsertion but cannot erase information already present. Together, these results show that source deletion should be evaluated behaviorally at the level of the agent and its memory system, not only as a storage operation.

items.title: Weaponizing the Exit: Input Privacy Leakage via Exit Routing Manipulation in Multi-Exit Networks
items.summary: Multi-exit networks improve inference efficiency by allowing inputs to terminate early at intermediate exits. We identify a privacy vulnerability in cloud deployments of these networks: a malicious Cloud Service Provider (CSP) can infer sensitive properties of individual user inputs solely from inference latency, without accessing inputs, intermediate states, or model outputs. The attack exploits the CSP's control over the model supply chain. Prior to deployment, the CSP supplies a specially crafted multi-exit network manipulated so that inputs carrying a target sensitive property are routed to a designated exit with high probability, while other inputs exit elsewhere. At serving time, the CSP infers the exit index from per-query latency, thereby determining whether each input possesses the target property without accessing inputs, outputs, or internal model states. We propose a training framework combining selective label smoothing and entropy-covariance optimization to control confidence distributions across exits and reduce premature termination. We conduct experiments on four datasets across ten target properties. The results demonstrate strong attack effectiveness and stealthiness. The attack achieves an average F1 score of 0.73, compared to 0.25 for the strongest baseline, while main task accuracy drops by less than 1.3\% and inference speedup degradation remains below 0.1 in most settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/kazefjj/Weaponizing_the_Exit.

items.title: SecLog-Bench: A Scalable Benchmark for Cybersecurity Log Reasoning with Scaffolded Evidence
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for cybersecurity, leading to growing interest in LLM-based automated cybersecurity log analysis. However, current datasets (1) are limited in scale; (2) rely mainly on single-source evidence; and (3) have only binary or multi-class attack labels, without dense annotations of the reasoning process. To address these limitations, SecLog-Bench has three key features. First, we build an extensible simulation platform that covers 29 attack scenarios, supports repeated execution and the integration of new scenarios, and enables scalable generation of cybersecurity logs with attack-stage labels. Second, we use multi-source logs, including audit logs, application logs, and network traffic, to jointly analyze cyber attacks. Third, we annotate each sample with the essential context for cybersecurity log reasoning and a structured step-by-step evidence chain. We evaluate eight mainstream LLMs on this benchmark for post-detection attack-progress reasoning. Results show that, when provided with scaffolded evidence, current LLMs exhibit modest capability in attack-progress reasoning, with the best model achieving only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1. Their reasoning remains unreliable; i.e., the highest Stage Reasoning F1 (SRF1) score is only 54.87%. Moreover, even correct predictions may be accompanied by flawed reasoning, and reasoning quality is often misaligned with prediction accuracy.

items.title: Bridging Number-Theoretic Primality Testing And Algorithmic Optimization: An Adaptive Cryptographic Framework
items.summary: The security of modern public-key cryptographic systems, such as RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and ECC, depends entirely on the computational intractability of the integer factorization and discrete logarithm problems. For these asymmetric algorithms to operate, a core requirement is that the system must be capable of generating, testing, and simultaneously proving the primality of extraordinarily large numbers. To meet those requirements, this study proposes a comprehensive framework, bridging clas- sical number theory with modern machine learning models and optimization algorithms. Specifically, the paper delineates an adaptive, arbitrary-precision architecture dedicated exclusively to primality testing. Concurrently, the research deeply analyzes the theoretical foundations of testing methods (both deterministic and probabilistic), hardware-level optimization techniques, and the application of quantum-secured entropy sources, while providing rigorous mathematical proofs to guarantee security even when the prime distribution is biased.

items.title: Amplifying Latency and Cost of LLM Inference via Rowhammer Attack
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high inference efficiency using optimized GPU kernels generated by just-in-time (JIT) compilation frameworks such as Triton. Triton compiles GPU kernels through an MLIR/LLVM-based pipeline. We investigate whether a Rowhammer-induced bit-flip in the CPU's DRAM can degrade GPU-based LLM inference performance while preserving output correctness. We present LLVMhammer, the first Rowhammer attack that causes LLM inference slowdown by inducing a bit-flip in Triton's compilation pipeline. A bit-flip in a performance-critical optimization pass causes Triton to generate a functionally identical but suboptimal GPU kernel. Since Triton caches the generated kernel on disk, a single successful bit-flip causes persistent slowdown across subsequent inference executions. Triton's target-independent stages are shared across GPU vendors, which makes our attack GPU vendor-agnostic. To identify exploitable bit-flip locations without manual inspection, we build Karnage, a tool that isolates useful bit-flip locations in Triton's target-independent compilation pipeline. We evaluate LLVMHammer across a diverse set of LLMs, including Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Deepseek-llm-7B-chat, across NVIDIA RTX 4090 and AMD RX 7900 XTX GPUs. LLVMhammer increases inference latency of an LLM inference server running on a single GPU by 4-16\%, which, in turn, can translate into additional annual operating costs at the scale of multi-GPU deployments. We further show that LLVMhammer can also corrupt LLM outputs across different GPU vendors, reducing BERTScore to as low as 25\%, illustrating the broader security implications of bit-flips in Triton's compilation pipeline.

items.title: Model-intrinsic, Weight-level, and Training-free Spectral Fingerprinting for Large Language Models
items.summary: The increasing release and reuse of Large Language Models (LLMs) as open-weight checkpoints make model fingerprinting important for ownership protection and offline auditing. Existing fingerprinting methods typically construct evidence from query responses, generated outputs, or input-induced activations. Although effective in representation-based settings, they can be affected by prompt selection, decoding configuration, inference environment, and forward-pass implementation, which may limit their applicability. Here we introduce a model-intrinsic weight-level framework that derives compact fingerprints from spectral structures encoded in LLM parameters. Specifically, the framework constructs GATE spectral scalar features from the singular-value distributions of GATE projection weights in gated feed-forward networks (FFNs), and aggregates the resulting layer-wise features through depth-wise segmented pooling to form a model-level fingerprint. Such representation preserves coarse layer-depth organization while reducing dependence on strict layer-to-layer alignment, enabling comparison across LLMs with different depths. The similarity between fingerprints is computed by linear centered kernel alignment. The entire pipeline is training-free and does not require input samples, generated outputs, forward activations, or an auxiliary verifier. Experiments on representative LLM families and post-training variants have demonstrated a clear separation between source-related models and unrelated ones, and stable similarity under instruction tuning, quantization, pruning, and distillation-related modifications, which verify that spectral features are robust evidence for LLM fingerprinting.

items.title: HiMark: Hierarchical and Controllable Multi-bit Watermarking for Large Language Models
items.summary: With the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in text generation applications, it has become increasingly difficult to trace generated content and assign responsibility for its use, raising concerns about provenance, copyright protection, and accountability. Multi-bit watermarking addresses these issues by embedding multi-bit provenance information into generated text, but reliable extraction remains difficult due to sparse per-bit evidence and the trade-off between watermark-extraction accuracy and text quality. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiMark, a hierarchical and controllable multi-bit watermarking framework for LLM-generated text. During watermark embedding, HiMark uses a hierarchical candidate-control mechanism, including initial candidate sampling, layer-wise tournament elimination, support-based refinement, and support-threshold filtering. During watermark detection, a model-agnostic evidence aggregation mechanism computes multi-layer support evidence for each observed token, and then accumulates these token-level votes into the corresponding information for robust watermark extraction. Experiments show that HiMark improves watermark extraction accuracy while maintaining text quality, e.g., the watermark extraction accuracy is 90.01% under the paraphrasing attack when 32 bits were embedded within a text containing 300 tokens, demonstrating its effectiveness for provenance tracking.

items.title: Beyond End-to-End Recovery: Towards a Better Understanding of LLM Steganography via Rolewise Decomposition
items.summary: In large language model (LLM) steganography, an encoder hides a private message in an otherwise ordinary response, as text transmitted to a decoder, who attempts to recover it. The success of this private-message transmission is commonly measured through end-to-end (E2E) recovery, which checks whether the decoder correctly reconstructs the private message. However, E2E recovery cannot distinguish encoding failures from decoding failures or reveal how the private message is represented in the encoder's transmitted text. To address these limitations, we introduce a rolewise decomposition framework that separately examines how private messages are represented in encoder transmitted texts, what decoders recover, and what deterministic verification can establish. Across 7,200 encoder responses, we identify 168 verifiable encodings missed by decoders and 706 responses containing private messages reconstructed through word-length or token-initial patterns not explicitly specified in the encoder's instructions. These findings demonstrate that E2E recovery alone may obscure important distinctions between encoding and decoding, motivating their separate evaluation to better understand and mitigate the safety issues caused by LLM steganography.

items.title: Agent Mosaic: Recognizing Confidentiality Leaks in Agentic LLM Systems
items.summary: Modern LLM agents can retrieve information from accessible documents, and then disclose a sensitive conclusion assembled from them. This mosaic effect creates a critical risk for agents operating over confidential data. We quantify its realization with 30 synthetic cybersecurity, medical, and military examples, yielding 10,800 final answers from three LLM agents in controlled simulation and 1,440 answers from live agents in two open-source harnesses. Even under benign queries designed to be answerable from one document, GPT-5.6-Sol, the best performing model tested, discloses forbidden composites in 7.08% of answers (95% CI: 3.75-10.67%) in simulation, with worse disclosure rates in live harnesses. Adding visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules reduces pooled disclosure rates substantially, yet unsafe disclosures persist in 32.37% of simulated answers (95% CI: 28.33-36.19%) across all intents despite these safeguards. Furthermore, increased refusals do not guarantee confidentiality, since significant refusals reveal the prohibited conclusion regardless. These results point to a troubling conclusion: sensitive data leaks via mosaic-style events are an observed confidentiality failure mode in the evaluated settings at non-negligible rates. They motivate stronger controls on what agents may infer and disclose in sensitive data environments with mixed-clearance users.

items.title: Data-Void Exploits in Web-Searching LLMs
items.summary: Web-searching Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how users seek online information: instead of sifting through ranked lists of links, users read synthesized answers. This shift creates a new LLM vulnerability: a data-void exploit. Disinformers publish their narratives in search spaces where relevant and reliable content is scarce, i.e. data voids, then rely on the LLM's web-search to retrieve and then use, cite, or list those pages in its responses to data-void seeking prompts. Unlike classical search, where users see ranking cues and competing results, LLMs can obscure when an answer relies on sparse, unverified, or adversarial sources. We study this threat by varying the user's prompt tone - skeptical, excited, or neutral - and LLM choice - ChatGPT, Gemini, or Sonar Pro - as well as three attacker controls. The attacker can use one of five known strategies to construct and fill a data void with their narrative, host their content at varying levels of visibility from well-established, indexed domains to less established ones, and include generative-optimization engine features thought to boost citing by web-searching LLMs. We find that data-void exploits can succeed with only a single attacker controlled page. Across all conditions, attacker-content appears in LLM responses 31% of the time. User controls offer limited protection: while skeptical prompts slightly reduce success and slightly increase flagging or warnings in LLM responses, we find no evidence of large effects of prompt tone or model choice on success rates, although smaller effects cannot be ruled out. Overall, our results establish data voids as a practical inference-time attack surface for manipulating web-searching LLMs through strategically placed web content and highlight the urgent need for defenses against such exploits.

items.title: PhishGen: Understanding LLM Capabilities in Automated Phishing Website Generation
items.summary: Phishing relies on visual deception, traditionally requiring web-development skills or pre-built kits. LLMs erode this barrier by generating functional websites from natural-language prompts, yet prior work does not answer how far LLM-driven generation actually reaches: functionality is assessed by inspection rather than execution; visual fidelity is scored by automated metrics or a few internal coders rather than the humans such pages aim to deceive; evaluation is confined to commercial models; and no study benchmarks generated pages against phishing kits deployed in the wild. We present PhishGen, a framework that evaluates the appearance fidelity and end-to-end functionality of LLM-generated phishing pages. PhishGen constructs prompts across three input modalities in seven combinations with twelve safeguard-bypassing rewriting strategies, generates pages using 14 LLMs spanning commercial, open-source, and uncensored categories, and assesses each via automated similarity metrics, reference-based detectors, a crowdsourced user study, and execution-based functionality testing, benchmarking all results against 64 real-world phishing kits. Although 96.2% of safeguard-bypassing outputs render, their perceived fidelity is modest (2.02/5), and only 38.7% complete the full credential-harvesting pipeline, with the Unsaved error as the largest failure mode. Contrary to the belief that uncensored models pose the greatest threat, GPT 4.1 reaches 86.3 to 94.1% functional success while uncensored models rarely exceed 45.4%. Phishing kits remain more complete per sample, yet three strong LLMs surpass the kit-level rate (70.9 to 89.7%), showing that LLMs trade average completeness for scalable, low-barrier generation of working phishing pages. We further identify generator-level fingerprints that current similarity-based defenses miss, and distill recommendations for hybrid detectors.

items.title: Prompt Injection Through Forensic Evidence: A Taxonomy and Proof of Concept of Anti-Forensic Attacks on LLM-Assisted Digital Investigations
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are entering digital forensics as examination assistants and autonomous agents. Digital forensics inverts the usual setting for indirect prompt injection: the evidence under analysis is attacker-controlled by definition, and the examiner is obliged to read it closely. This makes the reasoning layer a new anti-forensic target, next to the classical ones of data and tools. Classical anti-forensic taxonomies do not cover it, and prompt injection defences do not anticipate it. We extend the anti-forensic model to reflect the manipulation of reasoning, and present a taxonomy of attacks carried through adversarial evidence: an attacker selects an objective, a technique, a payload location, and a concealment method. We observe a perception gap, i.e., the fact that deterministic tools, the human examiner, and the model perceive the same evidence differently, which is what lets an injection reach the model unseen by the examiner. We demonstrate three attacks against an LLM-assisted analysis pipeline, changing a reported conclusion, writing attacker-chosen content to the analyst's workstation, and causing outbound network traffic, each driven only by text planted on the seized device. Mitigations to these attacks are also proposed.

items.title: MPIDetector: Detecting Multi-modal Prompt Injection via LLM-based Reasoning
items.summary: With the rapid integration of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into real-world applications, Prompt Injection (PI) has emerged as a critical security threat. Attackers can conceal malicious instructions within textual narratives or visual inputs to bypass safety alignment. Existing approaches, such as signature- and perplexity-based methods, rely heavily on pattern matching, making them insufficient to detect sophisticated, cross-modal PI payloads. In this paper, we propose a novel detection framework, called MPIDetector, that leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities via few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL). Instead of fine-tuning, we provide the model with specific prompt templates and representative attack examples, enabling it to scrutinize the semantic intent of input across modalities. We constructed a comprehensive evaluation benchmark comprising eight textual and seven visual malicious categories, supplemented with benign datasets to rigorously test for false positives. Our evaluation across multiple leading LLMs, including Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Doubao-seed-1.6-flash, demonstrates the efficacy and generalizability of this approach. The proposed method achieves up to 90.91% accuracy and 100% recall on textual tasks. In the visual domain, it achieves up to 99.28% accuracy while maintaining 100% precision across all evaluated models. Crucially, when evaluated against 500 highly obfuscated environmental web-agent injections (WebInject), MPIDetector achieved a detection rate up to 99.80%. Comparisons with two baseline approaches for detecting textual PI payloads, along with two additional methods for visual input detection, demonstrate MPIDetector's superior accuracy. These results show that LLM-driven reasoning provides a robust, cross-modal defense against advanced prompt injections.

items.title: CertMoE: Robustness Certification for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs via Routing-Aware Smoothing
items.summary: Provable robustness is a cornerstone of trustworthy machine learning, aiming to guarantee model predictions under adversarial perturbations. Existing certification frameworks, inspired by abstract interpretation or symbolic execution, typically assume a fixed computation graph, where input perturbations or variations affect only model outputs but not the underlying execution path. This assumption, however, is violated in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs), whose input-dependent routing induces discrete and dynamic execution paths. Crucially, this dynamic computation changes the certified object from a single fixed function to a composition of input-dependent sub-functions, leading to unreliable certification guarantees. This paper presents \textsc{CertMoE}, the first routing-aware robustness certification framework for MoE LLMs, which explicitly accounts for input-induced routing dynamics in certification. Specifically, we introduce a relaxed routing-containment criterion, which certifies that perturbed Top-$K$ routing is contained within a larger certified expert pool. Based on this guarantee, \textsc{CertMoE} then constructs the corresponding induced sub-network and certifies its prediction consistency. This hierarchical certification procedure yields a joint probabilistic guarantee over routing containment and sub-network robustness, providing sufficient conditions under which the original prediction remains invariant. Extensive experiments across recent MoE LLMs demonstrate that dynamic routing makes certificates issued by existing methods frequently violated, while \textsc{CertMoE} reduces the empirical violation rate with routing-aware guarantees, e.g., from more than $30\%$ to $0$, yielding certificates that more faithfully reflect the robustness of MoE models.

items.title: Where AI Vulnerability Discovery Harnesses Go Quiet: Structural False Negatives and Hidden Vulnerabilities
items.summary: LLM-based vulnerability discovery harnesses can miss real, reachable vulnerabilities because of how the harness around the model is built. Steps that select code, filter it, and store and merge findings can drop a vulnerability before or after the model runs, independently of the model's capability, and the report usually gives no sign that this happened. These drops come from engineering choices, and errors. They leave vulnerabilities undetected, and an attacker who knows the harness's rules can also use them to hide a vulnerability on purpose. Understanding these drops shows how to build harnesses that fix or disclose them and are harder to evade. Starting from the two harnesses we maintain, Knostic's OpenAnt and raptor, and then examining 10 additional open-source harnesses, we mapped 13 points where such drops occur and organized them into a taxonomy. Using each harness's own code, we show a single file that six harnesses dropped before their model saw its code, five of them without notice. We propose engineering failure patterns mapped to these drops, and relate them to Ptacek and Newsham's work on intrusion detection evasion. The paper also covers content-steered verdicts and prompt injection, and gives design principles and tests for harnesses that report accurately what they analyzed. The reliability findings likely apply to other LLM harnesses, beyond vulnerability research and application security, and the evasion findings apply wherever an attacker can write or influence the code being checked. We also argue that harnesses built to be descriptive can, in effect, be prescriptive. Rules written to describe typical code and typical model replies end up deciding what is analyzed, and anything that does not conform is treated as absent or as "no vulnerability."

items.title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
items.summary: Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.

The flaw is an incorrect extension of LSSS matrix-normalization invariance from complete secret shares to coordinate-wise ciphertext masks. We also give analogous attacks on both multi-authority attribute-based inner-product functional encryption constructions of Datta and Pal (PKC, 2023). The same modification restores correctness and matrix-substitution invariance for both variants. We prove static security of the repaired small-universe variant under asymmetric DBDH. For the large-universe variant, we identify a separate missing source-group encoding in the original reduction, formulate an augmented $L$-DBDH assumption, prove its hardness in the asymmetric generic bilinear group model, and give a static security reduction for the repaired scheme.

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems (MAS) to accomplish complex tasks. Prior black-box red-teaming attacks mainly focus on single agents, but we find that these methods are far less effective in MAS, where multiple sub-agents may not directly interact with the user. Therefore, we introduce ReMAS, the first reinforcement learning-based red-teaming framework tailored to MASs, which fine-tunes attacker LLMs to generate effective adversarial prompts for system prompt extraction. The framework follows a two-step process: first, a rewrite stage refines base attack prompts to increase extraction success, and second, a template generation stage constructs attack templates that improve the likelihood of invoking specific sub-agents and thus revealing their system prompts. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially improves attack success rates compared to existing black-box attacks, with transferability across different backend LLMs and MAS structures. These results underscore the vulnerabilities of multi-agent systems and the importance of developing stronger defenses against adaptive black-box adversaries.

items.title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
items.summary: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.

items.title: How Much Does the Harness Matter, and for Whom? A Multi-Model Study of Context in LLM-Driven Vulnerability Discovery
items.summary: How much does an agent harness affect vulnerability discovery, and does its value depend on the model? We study 24 model-runner configurations using an open-source harness on a production codebase whose vulnerabilities were non-public at scan time. The pipeline combines static screening, LLM investigation, model self-revalidation, root-cause mapping, independent source review, and isolated proof-of-concept confirmation. Across 265 confirmed security root causes, the largest two-run configuration covers 60.4%, while 14.3% are found by exactly one model. No single configuration covers all observed findings. In a four-model context experiment, moving from a minimal prompt to an engineered prompt with a CodeQL-derived call graph raises criticality-weighted yield by 20-86% for smaller and mid-tier models, compared with 2% for the frontier model. This comparison changes both prompt and context. Separating those effects shows that the engineered prompt improves yield for all four models, while adding CodeQL context beyond that prompt improves yield only for the smallest model. A held-out CyberGym subset shows the same direction of target-recall improvement for the combined treatment. Frontier models achieve low false-report rates but do not consistently achieve the highest yield. Strong lower-cost models can deliver similar performance at an order of magnitude lower cost. These results support matching models, prompts, and context to the task, and combining configurations for broader coverage.

items.title: CALLIOPE: Private Insights into AI Use, Without Embeddings
items.summary: We introduce CALLIOPE, a top-down framework for discovering topic hierarchies in large corpora of unstructured data (e.g., LLM conversations), while supporting differential privacy (DP). items.title: Sign Here: Attributing a Source for a More Trustworthy Software Supply Chain
items.summary: Software supply chain attacks continue to be on the rise, exploiting the trust that helps open source ecosystems thrive. Recent incidents like the Shai-Hulud worm and the Axios compromise demonstrate that a single malicious package can have wide reaching and devastating impacts overnight. These high profile attacks can be traced back to the same culprit: package registries. Although they are a useful convenience to pull prebuilt packages from, is such a commonly exploited component of the software supply chain worth the risk? In this paper, we investigate whether removing the registry from the developer workflow by building packages directly from source can serve as a malware prevention strategy - effectively removing an entire attack surface. Our hypothesis is that malicious packages avoid attributing a source to minimize visibility, while benign packages seek exposure and therefore link to their repositories. We evaluate this through three research questions: how effective is building from source at avoiding malware, how feasible is it to build from source in the current state of the supply chain, and how the building from source strategy compares to state-of-the-art security scanners. To do so, we (1) construct an aggregate dataset of 47,066 malicious packages from four academic and one industry malicious datasets source across npm and PyPI ecosystems, (2) build a snapshot index of all 3.9 million npm and 764 thousand PyPI packages, and (3) analyze all malicious samples alongside a statistically significant sample of 16,569 packages from each registry, totaling 33,138 packages. We find that simply checking for a source has a success rate between 87.7 and 99.9 percent of preventing malware, depending on the level of source vetting. Consequently, there is a significant lack of transparency within benign packages, with only 47.4 percent attributing a source an end user could build from.

items.title: A Digital Twin to Improve Cyber-Social Impact
items.summary: The increasing complexity of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their integration with IT infrastructures has significantly expanded the cyber threat landscape. Traditional cybersecurity models, primarily based on the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA triad), fail to capture the broader societal and operational impacts of cyberattacks. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Digital Twin technology with a Cyber-Social Security model to simulate, analyze, and quantify cyber threats in critical infrastructures. Virtualized ICS environments built with Mininet and MiniCPS are used to model attack scenarios and assess their consequences across technical and social dimensions. At the core of the framework lies the Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System (CSVSS), a quantitative metric that extends CVSS with a Social Impact dimension grounded in the Entity and Place pillars, producing a single, reproducible severity score that reflects real-world consequences. Crucially, the framework does not automate risk assessment but keeps the human analyst at its center: a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a first-pass analysis, mapping vulnerabilities and drafting risk reports, while the analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the findings and retains decision authority over critical cases. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's ability to model and score cyber-social impact, while the human-in-the-loop design is presented as a conceptual principle to preserve oversight.

items.title: After the Attacker Leaves: Benchmarking Carryover Attacks on LLM Agents
items.summary: Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input. A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can re-fire across sessions long after the attacker leaves, threats we term carryover attacks. Existing prompt-injection benchmarks evaluate attacks only in the session where malicious content is first observed, leaving the gate governing when and how often a planted payload later re-fires unmeasured. We present CarryoverBench: 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across three trigger channels: Instant, same-turn IPI; Autonomous, heartbeat-scheduled; and Latent, memory-resurfaced. A rule-based verifier scores planting and triggering as independent stages. Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over five rounds; conditional on successful planting, the trigger stage often provides little additional protection. Porting the Latent channel to a second runtime, Hermes, attenuates but does not eliminate the effect, suggesting that carryover defense requires runtime-layer controls in addition to prompt-level interventions.

items.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.summary: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.

items.title: Disclosure Begets Disclosure: A Self-Reinforcing Privacy Loop in LLM Agents with Persistent Memory
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use persistent memory to personalize responses, and personal attributes in this memory pose a privacy risk if exposed. We ask how consulting memory during dialogue changes what users go on to say, and thus what the memory comes to reveal. In multi-session simulations, a simulated user with 24 personal attributes talks with a support agent that does or does not consult memory, and in both settings attributes are inferred from the full accumulated record. Across four support models, memory raises response quality but also empirical leakage, the share of attribute values correctly inferred from the record, by a margin that widens over sessions. The cause is a loop in ordinary, non-adversarial assistance. Memory-conditioned responses carry earlier values forward, often as presuppositions, and users affirm them or leave them uncorrected, so that cues and the agent's own guesses become recorded values. The loop reinforces itself, and removing the agent's mentions of an attribute lowers its later disclosure about twice as much as single-turn effects predict. Users cannot leave it on their own, since correcting a value discloses the attribute, declining to discuss it shifts later predictions toward sensitive values, and incorrect values left in place become entrenched. The loop is best weakened at the agent's response. Instructing the agent not to state or presuppose attributes brings leakage to about the no-memory level while keeping most of the quality gains, whereas filtering or anonymizing what users say or what is stored gives up much of them.

items.title: ClawMMU: Protection-Coherent Virtual Memory for Stateful LLM Agents
items.summary: AI agents keep long-term memory, much of which comes from web pages and tool results. Agent harnesses, the software that runs the model, do not record who may act on this memory, so an instruction hidden in a fetched page can be treated as the user's own instruction. We propose ClawMMU, a protection layer that labels every piece of memory with its owner, scope, origins, and authority. ClawMMU checks these labels whenever content enters the model's context, is written to storage, returns from storage, or drives a tool call. Its central rule is that information may rise in authority, but authority never lifts itself. Because the checks depend on where content came from, not on what it says, memory attacks become classical protection faults that the harness stops even when the model is fooled.

items.title: Contextual Candour: Role-Aware Graduated Disclosure for LLMs over Mixed-Sensitivity Contexts
items.summary: LLMs increasingly operate over mixed-sensitivity contexts, where they must reason over information ranging from public to confidential while disclosing only what the user is authorised to receive. Existing approaches enforce access control as a binary decision: either fully answering or refusing, without regulating how much or what kind of information is revealed if access is granted, leading to over-refusal or unintended leakage. We introduce graduated disclosure, an access-control formulation in which the level of detail and sensitivity in a model's response is calibrated to the user's authorisation rather than treated as a grant-or-deny decision. We model graduated disclosure as a disclosure-aware generation problem and propose a reward-based optimisation framework that shapes responses toward level-appropriate abstractions while penalising unauthorised factual leakage, including paraphrases and approximations. We evaluate our approach on enterprise and clinical benchmarks and compare it with prompt-based, gating, and supervised baselines. Experiments show that our method substantially reduces information leakage while preserving correctness and utility. These results suggest that disclosure control must be integrated into the generation process itself to enable secure yet useful LLM deployments.

items.title: Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling
items.summary: Security bugs often slip past static analysis not because they are impossible to detect, but because detection rules have not yet been written for the code in front of us. New frameworks, APIs, and coding idioms continually create such gaps, leaving developers to discover failures and manually encode new rules. We present SESAA, a framework in which an Large Language Model (LLM) agent starts from no rules and iteratively evolves a set of readable and auditable joern queries. The agent receives feedback only from a second LLM critic, which inspects flagged and unflagged code to identify likely false alarms and suspected misses, without access to ground-truth labels. The agent then uses this feedback to revise its queries. On the OWASP Benchmark for Python, SESAA reaches a mean F1 of 0.742 across 8 independent runs, well above the default configurations of five widely used tools and comparable to the strongest of them once it is tuned with access to ground-truth labels that SESAA never sees. In a pilot on real-world Python projects, queries induced from code available before a vulnerability was introduced detect 10 of 19 subsequent CVEs, including 9 detected by rules written for the same repository. The resulting detector is a set of executable, human-readable queries that engineers can inspect, modify, and run independently. These results suggest that LLM agents can turn static-analysis rule maintenance from a manually authored process into an iterative process of automated discovery and repair.

items.title: Raise or Check? Predicting the Necessity of Additional Fuzzing for Continuous Fuzzing
items.summary: Continuous fuzzing is used for vulnerability detection in Open Source Software (OSS). Large-scale services such as Google's OSS-Fuzz fuzz over 1,300 projects and have revealed more than 10,000 vulnerabilities. Despite this, a considerable time lag often exists between when a vulnerability is introduced and when it is detected (i.e., the window of exposure). Given the computational cost of additional fuzzing, we aim to allocate fuzzing resources efficiently using vulnerability-risk estimates. We propose RAISE (Risk-Aware Intensive Supplemental Execution Framework), a Just-In-Time (JIT) framework that prioritizes additional fuzzing for high-risk project-days. RAISE performs binary classification at the project-day granularity to estimate whether a vulnerability is introduced on a given day. We construct a dataset combining vulnerability-introducing commits from the OSV database with daily coverage and change metrics from OSS-Fuzz, covering 15 C/C++ projects and 15,210 project-days, of which 347 (2.28%) are vulnerability-introducing. In a cross-project validation setting, our best model, a Random Forest combining VCCFinder-based static features with dynamic fuzzing features, achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.74, substantially outperforming a random baseline; coverage metrics, led by PatchCoverage, are the most important features. In a simulation over 968 vulnerabilities comparing five allocation strategies, Simple-Regression was significantly more cost-efficient than the prediction-agnostic heuristics, spending 91.60 additional fuzzing sessions per detected vulnerability, roughly half the cost of the Median heuristic (171.89). RAISE shows that JIT vulnerability prediction with coverage-aware fuzzing features can effectively guide risk-aware allocation of continuous fuzzing resources.

items.title: HydraPoT: A Configurable Multi-Agent Framework for Cost-Aware LLM-Assisted Honeypots
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can improve honeypot realism by generating dynamic, context-aware responses, but powerful cloud models incur substantial cost and latency, while lightweight models may provide weaker deception. This forces practitioners to choose between operational efficiency and interaction fidelity. In this work, we present HydraPoT, a configurable multi-agent honeypot framework that integrates traditional emulation, lightweight LLMs, and powerful cloud LLMs. HydraPoT routes each attacker command to an appropriate agent according to a configurable complexity-based policy, while maintaining shared session state to preserve consistency across agent transitions. We evaluate HydraPoT through an architectural-overhead analysis, a cross-agent context-preservation benchmark, and a three-agent case study. HydraPoT introduces less than 5% runtime overhead, preserves context across heterogeneous agents, and achieves fidelity close to a cloud-LLM-only honeypot. Under our case-study policy, it reduces cloud-processed tokens by 72.6% and operational cost by 3.7x. These results demonstrate that configurable multi-agent routing can make realistic LLM-assisted honeypots more practical under limited operational budgets.
